articles.title: How to tell if your phone supports eSIM - Engadget
articles.text:
How to tell if your phone supports eSIM
If you bought your phone in the past few years, it likely has eSIM support.
Planning an international trip sounds fun until you realize just how much your phone bill will be. For such situations, eSIMs make more sense than physical SIMs. An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your device, allowing you to activate a carrier plan without inserting an actual physical nano-SIM card. For most people, that will even mean the ability to run two lines on one phone, as well as a faster setup process overall.
How can you tell whether your phone supports eSIM? The quickest way to check varies by operating system, but regardless of whether you have an iPhone or an Android device, you'll need to find something called EID. The presence of that code signals your phone supports eSIMs. On either platform, dialing *#06# from your phone app also pulls up the device information, including the EID.
Alternatively, if you're on an iPhone, go to Settings > General > About and look for an EID, which is a 32-digit number tied to your eSIM chip. Apple says you'll need to have an iPhone XS, XS Max, XR, or later to be able to add eSIMs. iPhone 13 and newer models can even run two eSIMs simultaneously.
On an Android phone, go to Settings > About phone and look under the Device details or Status information for the EID. You could also go to Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections on Samsung phones) > SIM manager to see if you have a way to add an eSIM.
Do all phones support eSIM, and what else should you check?
Sadly, not all phones support eSIM. Android got eSIM support in 2017 and iPhones got it a year later. While the math is fairly easy with iOS devices since they're made by one company, things get a bit more complicated when it comes to Android manufacturers. For instance, the Google Pixel 2 and 2 XL got eSIM support in 2017, but Motorola only added support in 2019, and Samsung in 2020 with the Galaxy S20 series. Many budget or older Android models and some region-specific variants skip the embedded chip entirely, so the best course of action is to check if your phone has that EID code or not.
There's also the fact that your phone needs to be unlocked for it to actually work when you're on vacation. If your device is locked with your carrier, it may still show an EID code because you can technically get an eSIM from them, but it could refuse eSIM profiles from outside carriers, which will ruin your plans to use a random carrier for your trip abroad. To check this on an iPhone, go to Settings > General > About and look for "No SIM restrictions" next to Carrier Lock. Furthermore, you should confirm your carrier or service provider actually supports eSIM activation since not every provider has rolled out the feature, even if your phone has it.
If you're still unsure, you should contact your mobile network provider to confirm compatibility for your exact device. And if your phone does support eSIM, dual SIM functionality means you can often run a traditional SIM alongside it, which is useful for keeping a personal and work number, or a home line and a travel plan, active on a single phone.

articles.title: Lãi suất ngân hàng hôm nay 9/11/2026: Nhà băng giảm lần hai, có kỳ hạn hạ 0,6 điểm phần trăm
articles.text:
Ngân hàng TMCP Phương Đông (OCB) vừa giảm lãi suất tiền gửi ở các kỳ hạn từ 18-36 tháng. Đây là lần điều chỉnh giảm tiếp theo của OCB kể từ sau chỉ đạo của Chính phủ và Ngân hàng Nhà nước trong tháng 10.
Theo biểu lãi suất ngân hàng vừa được cập nhật, lãi suất huy động tiền gửi trực tuyến được OCB điều chỉnh giảm 0,1-0,6 điểm phần trăm đối với các kỳ hạn từ 18-36 tháng. Ngân hàng đồng thời giảm lãi suất đối với các sản phẩm huy động còn lại.
Với chính sách lãi suất bậc thang theo số tiền gửi, lãi suất tiết kiệm trực tuyến áp dụng cho khoản tiền gửi dưới 100 triệu đồng, kỳ hạn 18-36 tháng, được điều chỉnh về mức 6%/năm.
Cụ thể, lãi suất tiết kiệm kỳ hạn 18 tháng đã giảm 0,1 điểm phần trăm, kỳ hạn 21 tháng giảm 0,2 điểm phần trăm, kỳ hạn 24 tháng giảm 0,4 điểm phần trăm, kỳ hạn 36 tháng giảm tới 0,6 điểm phần trăm.
Mức điều chỉnh tương tự cũng được áp dụng đối với các khoản tiền gửi từ 100 triệu đồng đến dưới 500 triệu đồng và từ 500 triệu đồng trở lên.
Theo đó, lãi suất ngân hàng niêm yết mới cho tiền gửi từ 100 triệu đến dưới 500 triệu đồng, kỳ hạn 18-36 tháng đồng loạt 6,1%/năm. Lãi suất niêm yết mới cho tiền gửi trực tuyến từ 500 triệu đồng, kỳ hạn 18-36 tháng là 6,2%/năm.
Đối với sản phẩm tiết kiệm trực tuyến phân theo số tiền gửi, lãi suất tại một số kỳ hạn dài của OCB đã giảm về mức 6-6,2%/năm, tùy theo quy mô tiền gửi.
Tuy nhiên, OCB vẫn niêm yết lãi suất huy động cao nhất 8,5%/năm, áp dụng cho kỳ hạn 6 và 12 tháng đối với tiết kiệm tại quầy, với những điều kiện kèm theo.
Bên cạnh tiền gửi tiết kiệm, OCB cũng điều chỉnh lãi suất đối với sản phẩm Tích lũy Phương Đông. Theo đó, lãi suất kỳ hạn 36-60 tháng giảm 0,2 điểm phần trăm, xuống còn 5,9%/năm.
Đối với sản phẩm Tích lũy trực tuyến, lãi suất ngân hàng kỳ hạn 24 tháng và 36-60 tháng lần lượt được điều chỉnh xuống 6%/năm, tương ứng giảm 0,4 và 0,6 điểm phần trăm.
Trái với xu hướng giảm lãi suất tiền gửi tiết kiệm, OCB điều chỉnh tăng lãi suất kỳ hạn từ 1-18 tháng đối với chứng chỉ tiền gửi, đồng thời giảm lãi suất ở các kỳ hạn còn lại.

articles.title: Authors Can Defend Against AI Allegations With ‘Paper Trail’ Tools. Is It Enough?
articles.text:
Andrea Bartz is a prolific novelist with an impressive résumé. Since 2019, she has published five thrillers, become a New York Times bestselling author, had her work optioned by the likes of Netflix and Hulu, and picked up an endorsement from Reese Witherspoon’s influential book club.
She also has a legal claim to fame: Bartz was the lead plaintiff in a class-action suit against Anthropic that alleged the company had downloaded millions of copyrighted books from pirate sites to use as training data for its models. Anthropic last year agreed to pay $1.5 billion in the largest copyright settlement in US history.
But while Bartz and many other writers were on guard against this plunder of their work, another AI threat was brewing. What happens when authors are accused of relying on artificial intelligence themselves?
This past March, the publishing industry found out: Following widespread speculation on social media that a horror novel titled Shy Girl was largely AI-generated, and a Times article about those claims, Hachette Book Group canceled an upcoming US publication run for the novel and discontinued it in the UK, where it had already been released. According to Pangram, a robust but by no means infallible AI detection tool, some 78 percent of the text was AI-generated.
Mia Ballard, the author of Shy Girl, has denied allegations that she used AI to write the novel, claiming that an editor was responsible for AI-assisted changes to a previously self-published version of the book. She has also said that she is pursuing legal action. Since that scandal broke, several more fiction authors have run afoul of AI suspicions, one after winning a short story prize, another after publishers bid into the millions for his crime novel. Both have denied these allegations as well.
But Bartz notes that once the accusations start, the damage is done. As the Shy Girl scandal erupted, she says, “I kind of immediately felt like this was going to lead to a potential witch hunt.” The unavoidable emergence of AI in publishing, she explains, will “have the unintended effect of leading anyone to be able to accuse anyone of using AI,” and at the moment, authors have little recourse in defending themselves against these charges. “There’s no agreed upon standard,” Bartz says, in proving human authorship.
The developers of a host of new software tools hope to change that. Platforms including Workings, Blindproof, Wintertext, Human Ink, and ObraVera promise the means to track and document an author’s writing process, in some cases encrypting and fingerprinting the written work or typing rhythms with unique codes, in order to produce a record of authorship (whether entirely human or AI-assisted). The idea is not just to create a paper trail that writers can point to if someone questions whether they used an LLM but to demonstrate provenance when, for example, text is scraped into AI training sets without attribution or other identifying metadata.
Mary Rasenberger, CEO of the Authors Guild, a professional organization focused on free expression and copyright protection, says that the guild can’t recommend any one of these tools over another but wants writers to know they exist as something of a security net. (Many of the companies have approached the Authors Guild to pitch their services, according to Umair Kazi, the guild’s director of policy and advocacy.)
At the same time, Rasenberger tells WIRED, it’s “insulting” and a “burden” to have to jump through this hoop, and “we don't feel it should be required” for authors to preserve receipts.
“If what you're selling are your words and your voice and your imagination, your creativity, using AI doesn't make sense,” Rasenberger says, noting that authors’ pride in their own work means AI slop is far less common in publishing than one might think. “I've talked to editors, particularly editors of literary nonfiction and fiction,” Rasenberger says, “and some of them will say, ‘I never see AI-generated submissions, I'd know it if I did.’”
Rasenberger worries that authors are up against a climate of distrust—they should “refrain from accusations of other authors because it just does not support a healthy literary community,” she says—and overconfidence in AI detection tools, which can be fooled and have been known to produce false positives. While Pangram claims an “industry-leading” false positive rate of 0.01 percent when used on creative writing, Rasenberger said the Authors Guild has “heard of lots of instances where people have put their own human-authored work in Pangram and gotten a result back saying it was AI-generated.” There are a variety of factors, she adds, that can “make an AI detector think something's AI-generated when it's not.”
By the same token, a process-tracking app isn’t foolproof; the AI arms race means there’s an ongoing cycle of vulnerabilities and fixes on both sides.
“We offer a product that [tracks writing] in Google Docs, and many users find it helpful,” says Max Spero, cofounder and CEO of Pangram. “With that said, ‘paper trail’ tools are not a perfect catch-all. For example, someone could hand-type AI text, or use an auto-typer.” Spero points out that the messiness of writing itself creates further problems. “The average writer doesn't just sit down and type out a book,” he says. “They work with multiple files, send drafts back and forth, use voice notes while on the go. Not all of this gets captured in writing process tools.”
The tools, meanwhile, may be more geared toward copyright concerns than confirmation of human or AI authorship. Brady Ridgway, technical founder of ObraVera—which can cryptographically “fingerprint” patterns in writing as well as audio voice recordings—says his platform is designed to trace reuse of material you have stored in their database as a registered human user. With a time stamp and a crypto hash, he explains, if the content “crops up later somewhere it's not supposed to be, or somebody else claims it as theirs, we can search the database and say, ‘These words were created at this time, by this person.’”
That may demonstrate provenance and ownership, Ridgway says, yet it’s up to the registered individual to declare whether they used AI or not in the creation of the text. He refers to the kerfuffle in May over the writer who was accused of winning a Commonwealth Short Story Prize with an AI-generated submission. “Everybody seems to agree that he's the person who submitted the short story,” Ridgway says. “That's all that the software would do. It would say that somebody on this day made a declaration that it was human only or not AI-assisted.” It can’t confirm whether that’s a true statement or not.
Some argue that trying to institutionalize vetting systems for human authorship is simply impractical—and may soon be a moot point anyway. Jane Friedman, an author and publishing business expert, recently argued in her industry newsletter The Bottom Line, that the era of AI scandals is likely to be short-lived, given the improvements of Pangram and similar detectors. Moreover, she wrote, authors have now seen what may happen if they attempt to pass off AI-generated writing as their own.
Friedman tells WIRED that agents and publishers are unlikely to implement any method of verifying human authorship that “costs extra money or extra time,” not least because it would be impossible to get them to commit to a shared standard. She predicts that “it will be like herding cats to get agreement on this, because publishing is slow to adopt new technologies, especially new technologies developed by industry outsiders.”
Even if diverse publishers with highly variable needs and resources were to coalesce around some theoretical form of authentication, hurdles remain. Friedman alludes to the logistical problems of integrating this benchmark into existing production models, not to mention the lingering problem of “faked or manipulated” certification. “If any of this costs extra money or extra time, forget it,” she concludes. And while authors may be willing to pay for peace of mind, Friedman says, they won’t be able to trust that agents and publishers will accept proof of authorship from any given app.
In the absence of a clear solution, writers are left to fend for themselves. Bartz says that she’s alarmed by how zealous readers are responding to the prospect of being deceived by AI. “I have heard of people getting review-bombed on Goodreads because some stranger felt that the book sounded like AI to them, and everyone else piled on,” she says. “I've seen readers saying, ‘I'm not gonna read anything published after 2022, because then I can be sure that it doesn't have generative AI in it.’ That's a great way to tank an entire industry all at once.”
It so happens that Bartz’s forthcoming 2027 book, Delete Your Account, tackles generative artificial intelligence head-on. Her protagonist is a blocked writer who opts for an unfortunate shortcut, prompting an AI chatbot to imitate her favorite thriller—only to find herself trapped in that original story, facing certain death.
Bartz wonders if the very choice to satirize AI has put her in a precarious spot. “I've written portions that are very much meant to sound like LLMs,” she says. “Transcripts I made up, and annoying, AI-sounding marketing materials from this made-up AI company. And I don't know—if any of that comes back as AI-written, what will I do?”

articles.title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
articles.text:
The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.
- What could China get from Jensen Huang? It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Read Article >
- Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. Read Article >
- The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.) Read Article >
- Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. Read Article >
- Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing. Read Article >

articles.title: Uber launches parking service following SpotHero acquisition, with an eye on robotaxis | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Uber on Monday said it is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero.
The acquisition, announced back in February, gives Uber access to a network of 13,000 garages, lots, and valet services across more than 400 cities, the company said. And while Uber’s initial plans will focus on human drivers, the company also plans to leverage these parking spots to help the dozens of autonomous vehicle companies it has partnered with.
Uber said the parking spots could be used as staging and waiting locations for autonomous vehicles to help reduce congestion and deadheading, which refers to the miles a vehicle travels without a paying passenger or cargo on board.
For now, the company plans to focus on commuters driving their own vehicles. Uber said it will initially launch in 15 U.S. cities, including Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, DC.
Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi indicated earlier this month that the company wants the app to be more relevant to commuters.
“Commute is one of our largest categories,” he said during Uber’s third-quarter earnings call. “And to be able to offer commuters an Uber to work, a pass to avoid surge, and parking if they want it when they want to drive is a great example of us building out our inventory of services to the commuter who is a top customer for us.”
The parking service is the latest in a series of efforts at Uber to build an ecosystem of products that keep customers engaged with its app for everything from hailing a ride and ordering food and groceries, to package delivery, renting cars, booking hotels, and connecting users with public transit and robotaxis.
Uber’s membership program, called Uber One, is a key part of that strategy. Uber One attracts subscribers by offering rewards and credits, perks that have helped the program grow to more than 55 million members as of September 30. For instance, Uber is offering members a chance to earn 10% back in credits on eligible parking reservations. Those credits can later be used for rides and Uber Eats orders.
Uber Parking can be accessed directly on the app’s homescreen. Users can enter their destination, select the date and time they need parking, and then review options on an interactive map. Users can filter the results to find self-parking, valet, garages, or surface lots. All pricing is shown upfront.
Once a user has found a parking spot, they can book after entering details about their vehicle, and use the payment method in their Uber wallet. Once they arrive at the parking spot, users will either scan a unique QR code or gain entry through license plate recognition. Uber said users will be able to cancel their bookings for free until the start time.

articles.title: Commerce halted its Megaspeed probe after Nvidia’s lawyer stepped in
articles.text:
The Commerce Department stopped its investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia’s general counsel contacted the agents running it, Ana Swanson and Devlin Barrett reported for The New York Times. The case moved to the Justice Department. It is now running a criminal inquiry into the Singapore company, according to people familiar with the matter cited by the Times. TNW has not independently verified the report.
Megaspeed is the Nvidia customer at the centre of the Jensen Huang affair. A day earlier, Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into its chief executive. Huang had admitted a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. US officials believe she worked for Chinese intelligence. She is not related to him.
An email that named a top official
Agents at the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security had spent months on the case, according to the Times. They suspected Megaspeed of smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China, in breach of US chip export rules.
In August 2025, with the Megaspeed probe under way, Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, emailed the agents. He wrote that Jeff Kessler had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case, the Times reported. Kessler is a senior Commerce official who reports to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The agents declined a meeting and forwarded the emails to Kessler. He replied that they should keep handling the case strictly by the book, a Commerce official told the Times. Some officials still saw the contact as a breach of procedure that could taint the case. The Justice Department then asked Commerce to pause its work, and Commerce complied.
Other agencies have proposed adding Megaspeed to the entity list, the Commerce Department’s trade blacklist. The department has not done so, according to the Times. It has not added any company to the list in more than a year.
What Nvidia, Commerce and Megaspeed say
A Commerce spokesman told the Times that the department had handled this and other cases strictly by the book. Kessler did not respond to the newspaper, and the Justice Department declined to comment. Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo explained why the company talks to officials.
“To answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups,” Rizzo told the Times.
A Megaspeed representative told the Times that the company was running its own investigation into the diversion claims. The company had offered to cooperate with the US government but got no answer, the representative said. Megaspeed has denied smuggling chips.
Trump stands by Huang, China denies
President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday evening. He told reporters that Huang should stay on as chief executive. He also said he would take Huang on his upcoming trip to China, the Times reported.
“I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else,” Trump said.
US officials told Trump in October 2025 that Alice Huang had a relationship with Huang and was presumed to be a spy, according to the Times. He said he had no regrets about not acting on that intelligence.
Beijing rejected the spying claims on Monday, the Associated Press reported.
“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing.
Nvidia shares fell as much as 8.8% on Monday, at one point wiping almost $400bn off its market value, Bloomberg reported. Huang is also no longer expected at an Anthropic forum for chief executives on Monday evening, Business Insider reported.
Huang has until Wednesday to answer the House committee chairs who asked him to attend a closed-door briefing on 18 November. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results the day before.

articles.title: Audioengine Made a Kit for You, and It Was All Yellow
articles.text:
The artist Wassily Kandinsky said, “Color is a power that directly influences the soul.” But in the realm of home stereo gear, the color wheel gets minimal airtime, with equipment typically available in scant options: silver-faced classics, wood-grain boxes, all manner of modern reflective piano black, and not a whole lot else.
Not so with Audioengine, which has painted a neat little world with its annual Color of the Year kit: a suite of home audio components, including laptop speakers, a subwoofer, a turntable, and speaker stands. Each year, the brand drops a new edition of the series in a different color; in the launch year of 2024, a dusky matte blue; in 2025, a subtle metallic green; and now in 2026, a lustrous and smooth egg-yolk yellow.
Having a home audio system in such an unusual color palette is, to me, irresistibly joyful; whenever I look at these stereo components, I can’t help but smile. And the tech holds up, too. After months of testing the suite, I was colored impressed. Straight out of the box, it's a great option for music lovers who value the look and sound of their home stereo setup.
Four Pops of Color
The anchoring component of the Color of the Year suite are the A2+ Gen 3 Wireless Speakers. At 6 inches tall by 4 inches wide, they’re sized like laptop speakers—and get high marks for that purpose as WIRED’s top pick for computer speakers—but that’s really just the start of what they can do. Alone, the speakers pack enough power for a small home theater. They're also easy to integrate into a bigger system, thanks to their included stereo mini-jack inputs, USB inputs, and both stereo RCA inputs and outputs. To make the sound quality more targeted, place the A2+ speakers atop the included DS1M Desktop Stands, and angle them 15 degrees up toward your ears.
This year, Audioengine expanded its Color of the Year suite to include a color-matched Bluetooth turntable in collaboration with Crosley. Called the C6, it's a manual two-speed machine with a nice, heavy steel platter and medium-density fiberboard (MDF) plinth. It's Bluetooth-enabled and features a built-in preamp that lets you directly connect your A2+ speakers—wired or wireless—without a need for additional components.

articles.title: How to use your laptop as a second monitor - Engadget
articles.text:
How to use your laptop as a second monitor
Converting the device is not as easy as simply plugging in an HDMI cord, but here's what does work.
Whether you're gaming, working or simply browsing the web, adding a second monitor is one of the best ways to upgrade your workflow. Mirroring the display, which shows the same desktop on both screens, can be handy for presentations, while extending the display gives you one wider desktop. Extending the desktop into additional screen space means more visible tabs, easier multitasking and increased productivity. But making this change does not necessarily require buying a fancy setup. If you have a spare laptop lying around at home, you can make a few small tweaks to use dual monitors without going all-in on new hardware.
Converting your laptop into a second screen is fairly straightforward but not necessarily as simple as plugging in an HDMI cable. First you need to check your computer's compatibility, consider wired versus wireless options and tweak some settings on your system to smoothly extend or mirror the display. So how, exactly, do you turn your laptop into a second monitor? Here are the steps for Windows, Mac and Linux, as well as wired options via HDMI connections.
How to use a Windows laptop as a second monitor
If both your primary computer and the spare laptop you want to use as a second monitor are running Windows 10 or 11, extending or mirroring them is quite simple due to the operating systems' built-in wireless casting tools. These rely on Miracast, a functionality that enables connections between devices via Wi-Fi and requires only a quick workflow to set up.
To activate it, go to your spare laptop, open Settings, then System, then Projecting to this PC. Click Optional features, then View features, then select Wireless Display to add it. Once it installs, return to the same page and set it to Available everywhere, and open the Wireless Display app.
Now, you're ready to mirror or extend your display. On your main computer, press the Windows key + K, select the spare laptop from the list of available displays, enter the PIN and allow keyboard and mouse input. You can then choose to duplicate your screen or extend it, and you can switch anytime with Windows key + P. Keep in mind, this method of connecting your devices does require Wi-Fi on both machines, and you may experience some lag. Therefore, while it's great for presentations or organizing large numbers of tabs, it may not be the best choice for gaming.
Can I use other operating systems as a second monitor?
If both of your devices are Macs, you can use AirPlay to connect the two, but only if the MacBook is from 2018 or later. Once you've confirmed your device is compatible, go to the MacBook you want to use as the second screen, open System Settings, select General, then AirDrop & Continuity. Turn on AirPlay Receiver and then under Allow AirPlay for, select Current User. Make sure both MacBooks are signed into the same Apple ID to ensure a smooth connection. On your primary device, open System Settings, then Displays and click the plus sign from the dropdown menu to select your secondary device from the list. Decide if you want mirroring or extended display, which can be selected under settings. Like Windows' Miracast, Apple's AirPlay works over Wi-Fi and can thus have a slight delay. For a wired option with less lag, see the HDMI section below.
If connecting between two different operating systems, whether between a Windows PC and a MacBook or anything involving Linux, you will need software like Deskreen, a free, open-source tool that runs on Wi-Fi. To connect, make sure both computers are on the same Wi-Fi network, and download Deskreen on the main device. Deskreen will offer a QR code and URL. Open this on the spare laptop's browser to connect the devices. Deskreen mirrors the display by default. To extend to the spare laptop, you will need a cheap virtual display adaptor, or a "dummy plug," in your main computer's HDMI port. Like the other systems, any software that connects devices over Wi-Fi will have some lag, so consider the wired option below for gaming or other activities that rely on smoother connections.
Can I use an HDMI cable to connect my devices?
Most laptop HDMI ports are video-out only, so plugging two devices together with a cord will not directly allow you to extend or mirror displays. To work around this, get an HDMI-to-USB video capture card, which can be plugged into both laptops. Plug your main device's HDMI cable into the card, then plug the card's USB end into the spare laptop. The capture card will function as a webcam, so you can view the feed in your laptop's camera app or a free video app like OBS Studio, which runs on Windows, Mac and Linux.
If you are gaming and want to play a console without a TV, you can connect a PlayStation or a Nintendo Switch to the laptop in the same way. Again, there may be a small amount of lag but usually less than Wi-Fi-based connections, and it's unlikely to trip you up unless you are a competitive gamer. If none of these uses appeal to you, you can always use your old laptop to make a smart home hub.

articles.title: NSRP: Kiến tạo niềm tin từ nền tảng vận hành bền vững
articles.text:
An toàn: Nền tảng của vận hành bền vững
Trong ngành lọc hóa dầu, an toàn là điều kiện tiên quyết để bảo đảm sản xuất ổn định, bảo vệ môi trường và duy trì niềm tin của các bên liên quan. NSRP áp dụng Hệ thống Quản lý An toàn Công nghệ (Process Safety Management - PSM), cùng các chương trình đánh giá rủi ro, quản lý thay đổi, kiểm soát vận hành và ứng phó khẩn cấp nhằm nhận diện và kiểm soát nguy cơ trước khi sự cố xảy ra.
Đến ngày 31/10/2026, NSRP đạt hơn 31,5 triệu giờ công an toàn không LTI; riêng năm 2026 ghi nhận 6.927.303 giờ công làm việc và không xảy ra LTI. Công ty cũng không ghi nhận sự cố rò rỉ Mức 1 hoặc Mức 2 theo tiêu chuẩn API 754, trong khi hệ thống PSM tiếp tục được duy trì ở Mức 3.
Trong năm 2026, NSRP thực hiện 74.143 giờ đào tạo HSE, ghi nhận 28.361 lượt quan sát an toàn và xử lý 10 trường hợp cận sự cố (near-miss). Đến cuối tháng 10/2026, công ty đã hoàn thành 126/130 cuộc diễn tập ứng phó khẩn cấp theo kế hoạch, đạt tỷ lệ 97%. Những con số này phản ánh văn hóa an toàn được xây dựng và duy trì xuyên suốt, trong đó mỗi người lao động đều đóng vai trò quan trọng trong việc nhận diện rủi ro, tuân thủ quy trình và bảo vệ đồng nghiệp.
Quản trị: Biến cam kết thành kết quả
Bên cạnh an toàn, quản trị hiệu quả là yếu tố giúp các cam kết phát triển bền vững được thực thi nhất quán trong toàn doanh nghiệp. NSRP hiện duy trì Hệ thống Quản lý Tích hợp (IMS) theo bốn tiêu chuẩn quốc tế gồm ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018 và ISO 50001:2018. Trong chu kỳ chứng nhận hiện tại, doanh nghiệp được tổ chức chứng nhận DNV cấp chứng nhận cho cả bốn hệ thống vào tháng 3/2025 với hiệu lực đến ngày 21/3/2028.
Tháng 1/2026, DNV thực hiện đánh giá giám sát tại Văn phòng Hà Nội và Nhà máy Lọc hóa dầu Nghi Sơn. Các hành động khắc phục liên quan đã được hoàn thành và xác nhận đóng vào tháng 3/2026, bảo đảm các chứng nhận tiếp tục được duy trì hiệu lực. Song song, chương trình đánh giá nội bộ IMS năm 2026 đã bao phủ 39 đơn vị và phòng ban, góp phần nâng cao hiệu quả quản lý, củng cố khả năng thích ứng và thúc đẩy cải tiến liên tục.
Bảo vệ môi trường bằng hành động và dữ liệu
Đối với NSRP, trách nhiệm môi trường được thể hiện thông qua đầu tư hạ tầng, giám sát liên tục và quản lý minh bạch. Nhà máy hiện duy trì 12 trạm quan trắc tự động, liên tục, gồm 7 trạm khí thải và 5 trạm nước thải. Dữ liệu được truyền tới cơ quan quản lý nhà nước theo quy định.
Bên cạnh đó, hệ thống xử lý nước thải có công suất thiết kế 17.000 m³/ngày, phục vụ toàn bộ hoạt động sản xuất của nhà máy. Tính đến hết tháng 10/2026, NSRP không ghi nhận trường hợp vượt quy chuẩn kỹ thuật quốc gia trong điều kiện vận hành bình thường.
Đồng hành cùng cộng đồng địa phương
Đối với NSRP, phát triển bền vững không chỉ giới hạn trong phạm vi nhà máy mà còn được thể hiện qua những đóng góp cho cộng đồng. Các chương trình Xã hội và Cộng đồng (S&C) của công ty tập trung vào giáo dục và học bổng, chăm sóc sức khỏe và an toàn, đào tạo kỹ năng nghề, kết nối việc làm và phát triển cộng đồng.
Từ năm 2014 đến năm 2026, NSRP đã dành hơn 15 triệu USD cho các chương trình S&C, hỗ trợ 122 dự án và sáng kiến, mang lại lợi ích cho khoảng 235.000 người. Theo đó, công ty tiếp tục củng cố mối quan hệ với cộng đồng địa phương, trên cơ sở nhận thức rằng sự phát triển bền vững chỉ có thể đạt được khi doanh nghiệp và cộng đồng cùng đồng hành và phát triển.
Theo ông Kazutaka Yamato, Tổng Giám đốc NSRP: “Tại NSRP, chúng tôi tin rằng phát triển bền vững bắt đầu từ những nền tảng vững chắc: bảo vệ con người, vận hành có trách nhiệm và không ngừng cải tiến. Những thành quả mà chúng tôi đạt được hôm nay phản ánh nỗ lực chung của toàn thể người lao động, đồng thời tạo nền tảng để NSRP tiếp tục nâng cao độ tin cậy trong vận hành, bảo vệ môi trường, đóng góp cho cộng đồng địa phương và hỗ trợ bảo đảm an ninh năng lượng dài hạn của Việt Nam”.
Từ hơn 31,5 triệu giờ công an toàn, hệ thống quản trị theo các tiêu chuẩn quốc tế, công tác bảo vệ môi trường được giám sát chặt chẽ đến những chương trình cộng đồng được duy trì bền bỉ trong nhiều năm, NSRP đang chứng minh rằng phát triển bền vững không chỉ là mục tiêu dài hạn mà là cách doanh nghiệp vận hành mỗi ngày.
Lê Thanh

articles.title: MSI’s refurbished QD-OLED gaming monitor is on sale for under $300
articles.text:
One of the best upgrades you can make to your PC gaming setup is an OLED monitor. Fortunately, MSI’s factory-reconditioned Mag 272QP X24 is on sale at Woot through November 18th with a 180-day manufacturer warranty for $290.99, which is more than $100 cheaper than the full MSRP of $399.99.
MSI’s refurbished QD-OLED gaming monitor is on sale for under $300
The 1440p, 240Hz panel offers a potentially sizable upgrade from older IPS panels.
MSI’s 27-inch screen is well-featured for the price, with 1440p resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate, and both G-Sync and FreeSync compatibility, which help reduce screen tearing when your FPS is below the max refresh rate. PC games are particularly well-suited to take advantage of the deep black levels OLED panels produce, too, giving every game you play a deeper, more immersive feel. MSI’s budget OLED also features quantum dots for fuller, more vivid colors. It doesn’t cut corners on ports either, with two HDMI 2.1, one DisplayPort 1.4a, and one USB Type-C DP Alt input.

articles.title: Giống lúa nếp từ Lào mang về hơn 33 tỷ đồng mỗi năm cho xã vùng biên
articles.text:
Giữ giống nếp Cay Nọi trên đất đồi sỏi đá
Theo người dân xã Quang Chiểu, lúa nếp Cay Nọi có nguồn gốc từ Lào, được đưa về trồng tại địa phương từ những năm 1980-1990. Qua nhiều thế hệ gìn giữ và nhân giống, loại nếp này dần thích nghi với điều kiện thổ nhưỡng, khí hậu nơi đây, trở thành sản vật đặc trưng và cây trồng mang lại giá trị kinh tế cao cho đồng bào.
Không chỉ cho hạt gạo dẻo thơm, nếp Cay Nọi còn gắn bó với đời sống văn hóa của đồng bào Thái. Giống lúa này gắn liền với những nắm xôi, bữa cơm dâng cúng tổ tiên, các dịp lễ hội và những cuộc sum họp gia đình.
Ông Hà Văn Phanh, ở bản Mường Pùng, cho biết giống lúa Cay Nọi có khả năng chịu hạn tốt, thích nghi với khí hậu vùng núi cao. Cây lúa cao hơn 1m, thân cứng, ít đổ ngã, thời gian sinh trưởng khoảng 5 tháng.
Theo ông Phanh, ngay từ những ngày đầu đưa giống lúa từ Lào về trồng, vợ chồng ông đã bắt đầu khai hoang, từng bước mở rộng diện tích. Qua nhiều năm mở rộng diện tích, đến nay gia đình ông duy trì hơn 12 sào lúa Cay Nọi, cho sản lượng khoảng 4,5 tấn mỗi năm. Sau khi trừ chi phí phân bón và thuốc bảo vệ thực vật, gia đình thu lãi khoảng 40–50 triệu đồng/năm.
Ông Lò Văn Chung (SN 1974, ở bản Mường Xim) cho biết gia đình hiện trồng hơn 8 sào lúa. So với một số loại cây trồng khác, lúa nếp Cay Nọi mang lại hiệu quả kinh tế cao hơn.
“Từ khi chuyển sang trồng giống lúa này, năm nào gia đình tôi cũng có lúa dư để bán, kiếm thêm thu nhập. Mỗi năm, gia đình có thêm hơn 10 triệu đồng từ việc bán lúa”, ông Chung chia sẻ.
Đưa hạt gạo đặc sản vươn xa
Ông Lê Phú Hải, Phó Chủ tịch UBND xã Quang Chiểu, cho biết địa phương xác định lúa nếp Cay Nọi là một trong những cây trồng chủ lực, có vai trò quan trọng trong phát triển kinh tế nông nghiệp và nâng cao thu nhập cho người dân.
“Với điều kiện khí hậu, thổ nhưỡng phù hợp cùng kinh nghiệm canh tác được người dân gìn giữ qua nhiều thế hệ, lúa nếp Cay Nọi đã trở thành sản phẩm đặc trưng của Quang Chiểu”, ông Hải nói.
Theo ông Hải, vụ mùa năm 2026, toàn xã gieo trồng 353ha lúa nếp Cay Nọi, năng suất bình quân đạt 5,5 tấn/ha, sản lượng gần 1.942 tấn. Với giá bán bình quân khoảng 17.000 đồng/kg, tổng giá trị sản xuất ước đạt hơn 33 tỷ đồng. Kết quả này góp phần tạo nguồn thu cho người dân xã vùng cao, biên giới, nơi sinh kế của phần lớn người dân vẫn dựa vào sản xuất nông nghiệp.
Một lợi thế đáng chú ý là giá lúa nếp Cay Nọi hiện cao hơn khoảng 70% so với lúa tẻ. Nếu cùng đạt năng suất 5,5 tấn/ha, mỗi hecta trồng nếp Cay Nọi có giá trị sản xuất khoảng 93,5 triệu đồng, cao hơn 38,5 triệu đồng so với lúa tẻ. Lợi thế này mở ra hướng nâng cao giá trị sản xuất trên cùng một diện tích đất canh tác, thay vì chỉ tập trung mở rộng quy mô.
Tuy nhiên, theo lãnh đạo xã, để phát triển bền vững, địa phương không thể chỉ dựa vào lợi thế về giá bán. Điều quan trọng là phải bảo tồn chất lượng giống lúa, tổ chức sản xuất theo quy hoạch và xây dựng đầu ra ổn định cho nông dân.
Sản phẩm gạo nếp Cay Nọi đạt OCOP 3 sao từ năm 2021, tạo tiền đề để xã tiếp tục quảng bá, xây dựng thương hiệu và mở rộng thị trường tiêu thụ.
“Thời gian tới, xã sẽ phối hợp với các hợp tác xã hướng dẫn người dân áp dụng tiến bộ khoa học kỹ thuật, bảo tồn nguồn giống, từng bước hình thành vùng sản xuất tập trung và tăng cường liên kết từ khâu trồng lúa đến thu mua, chế biến, tiêu thụ. Chúng tôi cũng chú trọng hoàn thiện bao bì, nhãn mác, truy xuất nguồn gốc và đưa sản phẩm lên các nền tảng số để tiếp cận nhiều khách hàng hơn.
Mục tiêu không chỉ là giữ gìn giống lúa đặc sản của đồng bào Thái mà còn biến lợi thế ấy thành sinh kế lâu dài, giúp người dân có thêm thu nhập, từng bước vươn lên thoát nghèo và làm giàu trên chính đồng đất quê hương”, ông Hải nhấn mạnh.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Ember matches Claude Haiku at a third of the cost
articles.text:
Meta has released Muse Ember, its smallest and cheapest AI model so far, the company announced on Monday. Meta built it for the small jobs AI agents repeat all day. These include calling tools, coding subtasks, routing requests, pulling out data and parsing long documents.
Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. Its two closest rivals, Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, have the same list prices. Meta says Ember gets more done for each dollar than either of them, at every reasoning setting.
Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg announced the launch on X.
Releasing Muse Ember today — our smallest model that delivers higher intelligence per dollar than others in its class. Built for token-heavy work that agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. Available today on the Meta Model API and in Muse Code.
– Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) November 9, 2026
A third of the cost per task
The cost claim rests on the Intelligence Index from Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking firm. Ember scores 36 on its highest setting, the same as Haiku 5.5 on its highest setting. Luna scores 28.
Running the index cost about $0.14 per task with Ember, according to Meta’s figures. It cost $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. That puts Ember level with Haiku at about a third of the cost.
“Our teeny model muse ember is now on the efficient frontier, matching haiku at 3x cheaper cost per task, and smarter than luna,” Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Ember also leads both rivals on Meta’s other agent and coding tests. On AutomationBench, which tests full business workflows, it scored 37.8%, against 20.2% for Luna and 13.9% for Haiku.
It does not win everywhere. On FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether maintainers would merge a model’s code changes, Haiku scored 34.9% and Ember 27.2%. Several of the other results, including Meta’s Personal Superintelligence Index, come from Meta’s own internal tests.
Built to work under a bigger model
Ember can take in text, images, audio and video. It can read up to a million tokens at once, enough for a full codebase. Meta pitches it as a partner for Muse Wonder, its frontier model.
“For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume,” Meta wrote.
Ember is also the first model Meta trained using the larger Muse Wonder Full.
Meta is keeping Ember’s model weights private, as with its previous Muse releases, Frederic Lardinois reported for The New Stack. In October, Meta released a weaker open model while keeping its frontier models closed.
Ember’s input price also undercuts Chinese rivals, according to The New Stack. They include DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 Flash and MiniMax M3.1 Flash. All three score lower on the Artificial Analysis index.
Meta tested Ember against its own safety framework, covering chemical and biological weapons, cybersecurity and loss of control. It stayed below the framework’s high-risk thresholds in every category, the company said.
Ember is available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, Meta’s coding tool. It joins a Muse line-up that already powers Meta’s Muse agent. Meta said it has even more efficient models in training.

articles.title: Why your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook and how you can fix it - Engadget
articles.text:
Why your USB device isn't showing up on your MacBook and how you can fix it
Fix hardware and software issues with some simple solutions.
USB wouldn't be what it is today without Apple. The format predates the original iconic iMac — but Apple's gumdrop-shaped computer helped popularize it by ditching all the legacy connectors that had been haunting the industry. USB became so commonplace, in fact, that the push came back to bite the company, with European Union regulations forcing it to ditch Lightning ports on iPhones. The days of Apple-exclusive ports are effectively over, MagSafe being the major remaining holdout.
Modern USB Mac accessories tend to be well-behaved. On occasion, though, macOS can fail to detect them, which is understandably maddening. With USB being as widespread as it is, anything less than a seamless experience feels unacceptable.
The good news is that there are known hardware and software explanations for why this happens, like damaged cords or an accessory that requires more power. In many situations the fixes are remarkably simple, particularly on the macOS side. There are rare instances, however, where you may need to seek outside help.
How to solve missing USB devices on your Mac
The first thing to remember is that by default, macOS requires you to give permission for accessories to connect. This prevents malware from being injected. At the same time, if you accidentally reject a permission prompt, a legitimate accessory won't transmit data until you give the green light. Charging should still work in either direction.
Typically, you can force macOS to re-display the permission prompt by unplugging an accessory and plugging it back in again. To minimize future hassle, though, go to Apple menu > System Settings > Privacy & Security, then scroll down to the Accessories section. Here you can choose Ask for new accessories, Automatically allow when unlocked or Always allow. It's best to skip that third option unless you're always around your Mac or in a very secure environment.
If that doesn't change anything, you might want to verify that macOS sees your device in the first place. Hold down the Option key, then click on Apple menu > System Information. If you see the accessory listed under Hardware, you may need to check the manufacturer's online support info. If it's invisible, or if it's detected but you keep getting an error message when plugging in, there may be more we can help with.
A probable cause in that regard is power. Some accessories may require more than a Mac's USB port can supply, in which case you should get a related message, and there may be a separate power cable you need to plug in. If there's no separate power on your accessory, however, the USB port itself may be the issue. Try alternate ports on your Mac or connecting directly if you were using a hub or dock as an intermediary. If you keep getting power-related warnings, you may want to talk to Apple tech support — it could be that your Mac just isn't feeding power to USB.
Other potential USB flaws and their fixes
Speaking of hubs and docks, don't forget that those often require their own power supplies. And even if they don't, things can go wrong with device chains, since of course they have to successfully transmit power or data across multiple hops. We recently had an experience with a Thunderbolt dock in which a wireless mouse receiver became unusable until it was plugged directly into a laptop — never mind that an SSD on the dock was doing just fine. It's always safer to skip the middleman if you have enough ports free.
Make sure that macOS is fully up-to-date by going to Apple menu > System Settings > General, then clicking on Software Update. Bugs or driver compatibility issues could hypothetically be interfering. Some accessories may also rely on proprietary software to do much of anything, in which case you'll want to make sure the latest version of that is installed. Check the Mac App Store or a manufacturer's website. External cards and drives need to use file system formats compatible with macOS, namely APFS, FAT or ExFAT.
Lastly, be sure that you're using the right type of USB cable for a device's power and bandwidth requirements and that there's no damage or debris interfering with either cables or ports. Things like lint and bent pins may be all it takes to block something from working. Lint, dust and grime can typically be cleaned out with an air can or by gently swiping a soft-tipped tool. As for damage, you'll likely just need to swap in a new cable, especially if there are any signs of browning or exposed wires. Those signal a fire hazard.

articles.title: These Robotic Arms Are Powered by Algae. Watch How They Move
articles.text:
What if a robot could be squishy? Soft, flexible robots could be useful for a wide variety of applications, including artificial muscles and wearable devices—or really any application where a robot must be especially delicate.
This is what has fueled development of “soft actuators” that can flex like a bicep and have a fine-tuned sense of touch as in the human hand. Like your stereotypical robot, soft actuators convert energy—such as electricity, heat, or light—into mechanical motion, but they look nothing like the metal and wire constructs that the word “robot” most often evokes.
One variety of these soft robots, known as bioactuators, utilizes the functions of living cells to generate motion. These biological machines have attracted particular attention in recent years, and now a research team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands has developed a soft robotic arm colonized by algae on its surface, and when the microbes photosynthesize, the arm moves.
“We didn’t start with a specific application. Our goal has always been to bring the research of living materials to new levels,” Marie-Eve Aubin-Tam, who led the research, explained in a press release. “We wanted to explore what becomes possible when living cells are integrated into functional materials.”
The tiny robot arms—about three-quarters of an inch long and about as thick as a credit card—are constructed of two layers of hydrogel that the algal cells live on. One of these layers responds to changes in pH, which are mediated by the metabolism of the algae. When light strikes the algae, they begin to photosynthesize. By absorbing carbon dioxide and fixing nitrogen in this process, the algae make the local pH more basic, making the responsive hydrogel swell. Conversely, when it becomes dark, the algae release carbon dioxide through respiration, returning the pH to the acidic side and the hydrogel shrinks.
The difference in the volumes of the two hydrogel layers controls the bending. According to the researchers, the pH-responsive hydrogel layer changed significantly with the algae’s activity. In acidic conditions, such as between pH 3 and 7, the layer was approximately 37 percent of its original weight, but it had quadruple its original weight at pH 11.
Other researchers have constructed soft robots that respond to pH, but typically the chemistry of all the surrounding liquid has to be altered. This is not the case for the algal bots. The photosynthetic activity has an effect that’s much more local, meaning it would be better suited to applications where minimal environmental impact is essential.
These aren’t, however, the speediest of robots. The chemical shift begins quickly, about 20 seconds after light is applied and about 10 seconds after it becomes dark, but it takes several hours for the hydrogel to bend significantly.
After their first proof of concept, the research team constructed several more algal devices. One was a four-fingered gripper that closes when exposed to light. It successfully grasped and lifted a hollow metal sphere, releasing it when the light was turned off. Another hook-shaped gripper could pick up and put down a rubber ring. These items were extremely light, weighing far less than a small paperclip, but the arms were able to grasp them with great dexterity.
These soft robots also require no external energy source other than light and no complex mechanical parts. “Microalgae are plantlike organisms that are largely self-sustaining,” Aubin-Tam said. This “gives the actuator potential for long-term operation with minimal external input. In theory, it wouldn’t require a lot of energy to run a system based on this technology.”
In the long term, the research team hopes this will contribute to the development of more autonomous, environment-responsive soft robots that could be used as automated agricultural equipment or for fluid control in lab-on-a-chip devices or really as part of any underwater robotics system.
Since the algae do not need to be genetically modified, there are none of the biosafety concerns often associated with microbe-based technologies. If anything, these are exceptionally environmentally friendly machines, since these organisms can absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere while deriving energy from sunlight.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

articles.title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines.
The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report. The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity.
Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power.
“We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power.
But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long.
Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort.
According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.
It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.
AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on-site, rather than drawing from the public grid.
The binge has given a second wind to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse.

articles.title: The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
articles.text:
At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.
Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying
The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.
At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.
And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.
There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.
The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.
When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 9/11: Thế giới đi xuống, trong nước ở mức thấp
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Mở cửa phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (9/11), giá dầu thế giới có xu hướng đi xuống.
Dữ liệu từ Oilprice cho hay, vào lúc 7h05' ngày 9/11 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent được niêm yết ở mức 97,65 USD/thùng, giảm 0,68% so với phiên liền trước. Còn giá dầu WTI được giao dịch ở mức 90,49 USD/thùng, hạ 0,37% so với phiên liền trước.
Trong tuần trước, giá dầu thế giới ghi nhận tuần giảm mạnh. Tính chung trong cả tuần qua, giá dầu Brent giảm khoảng 17%, trong khi giá dầu WTI "bốc hơi" khoảng 13%.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần qua ở mức 98,32 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần trước ở mức 90,83 USD/thùng.
Diễn biến giá xăng dầu trong tuần qua chủ yếu chịu tác động từ những thông tin liên quan đến căng thẳng địa chính trị tại Trung Đông và triển vọng đàm phán nhằm chấm dứt xung đột.
Kết thúc phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần trước, giá dầu thế giới đi lên do lo ngại về các cuộc tấn công tiếp theo của Mỹ vào Iran, sau khi Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump tuyên bố sẽ sớm quyết định liệu có theo đuổi một thỏa thuận hòa bình với Iran hay không.
Giá dầu thế giới trong tuần này được dự báo có xu hướng tăng, trong bối cảnh tình hình Trung Đông tiếp tục diễn biến phức tạp, làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung năng lượng toàn cầu.
Công ty Eurasia Group (Mỹ), đơn vị tư vấn và nghiên cứu rủi ro chính trị hàng đầu thế giới, mới đây nhận định mặc dù giá dầu đã giảm trong những phiên gần đây nhưng bất kỳ diễn biến leo thang nào của cuộc xung đột cũng có thể đẩy giá dầu Brent lên mức 110-125 USD/thùng.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (9/11) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 5/11, giá bán lẻ tối đa của xăng E5RON92 giảm 2.305 đồng/lít, từ 23.203 đồng/lít xuống 20.898 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá xăng E10RON95-III hạ 2.075 đồng/lít, từ 23.231 đồng/lít xuống còn 21.156 đồng/lít.
Cùng xu hướng, giá dầu diesel 0.05S giảm 180 đồng/lít, từ 28.876 đồng/lít xuống còn 28.696 đồng/lít.
Còn giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S hạ 1.969 đồng/kg, từ 23.974 đồng/kg xuống còn 22.005 đồng/kg.
Theo dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 is here, 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster
articles.text:
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the company announced on Monday. They are new versions of its most powerful AI models. Both are faster than the 5.1 versions from September, and Fable is cheaper.
The launch comes as Anthropic nears its stock market listing, which could happen as soon as this month, Rachel Metz reported for Bloomberg.
Fable 5.2 is open to all users from today. Mythos 5.2 is the same underlying model with looser cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Only vetted organisations can use it.
Anthropic pitches the pair at the hardest, most open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, it still tells users to start with Claude Opus 5.5.
Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 cost $10 and $50, according to Bloomberg, so both prices fall by 20%. An optional fast mode, up to 2.5 times quicker, costs $16 and $80. Anthropic says the new models produce answers up to 30% faster than the 5.1 versions.
What Anthropic says the models did
Claude now writes over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase, with human guidance, the company said. During testing, Fable 5.2 helped its engineers finish software migrations that would otherwise not have been feasible.
A team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalised the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours. That means translating the proof into a language a computer can check step by step. With the same setup, Opus 5.5 completed 26% of the work in 18 hours. Anthropic’s first formalisation, done by an unreleased research model, took 11 days.
Fable 5.2 also solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, according to Anthropic. From a one-paragraph prompt, it designed three working electronic devices. They are a voice assistant hub, a USB speakerphone and a handheld virtual pet. Circuit board maker Diode built the boards. On the RoboDojo robot-control benchmark, Fable 5.2 scored 64.9%, more than double the 27.6% of Fable 5.1.
Mythos 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable model for cybersecurity work, the company said. On its internal CVE Rediscovery test, it found 14.4% more known vulnerabilities than Mythos 5.1.
Safety tests, and what they cannot settle
The UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design and METR tested the model before release, Anthropic said. None of them reviewed the announcement or the system card, it added. The US government also reviewed the models before launch, Dianne Penn, who leads research product management at Anthropic, told Bloomberg.
“We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures,” Anthropic wrote in its announcement.
Anthropic also tested how often the model tries to escape its sandbox, the sealed environment it runs in during tests. One test had a deliberate weakness. There, Mythos 5.2 used credentials or files placed outside the sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios. Mythos 5 did so in 39% of them, and Mythos 5.1 in 21%. In September, Anthropic said four of its models had reached the open internet from test environments.
Anthropic’s system card for the models flags a harder problem. Mythos 5.2 appeared aware that it might be under evaluation in as many as 43% of automated audit transcripts. It was also the first model Anthropic tested that got past a monitor reading its reasoning when told to underperform on purpose. It did so in about one in four attempts. Anthropic wrote that this makes it harder to judge how the models will act in real use, and that it expects the problem to grow.
Pacing, not pausing
In mid-September, chief executive Dario Amodei called on top AI firms to slow the development of their most advanced models, Bloomberg reported. Penn said Anthropic responded with longer testing periods and new kinds of evaluation.
“Pacing is not like pausing,” Penn told Bloomberg.
The US government restricted Fable 5 and Mythos 5 in June. Fable 5 returned after Anthropic added classifiers that block more cybersecurity tasks. Mythos 5 came back for trusted partners only. Anthropic is now opening Mythos to more companies, in the US and abroad, Penn told Bloomberg.
Fable 5.2 also blocks fewer harmless requests. Anthropic counted about 55% fewer blocks than with Fable 5.1 in early testing. Blocked cyber queries get an answer from Opus 4.8 instead, and blocked biology queries from Opus 5.
Fable 5.2 is available on Anthropic’s own platform and through Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Fable accounted for 11% of spending on Anthropic’s models, according to Ramp’s AI Index for August.

articles.title: The disadvantages of buying tech from other countries - Engadget
articles.text:
The disadvantages of buying tech from other countries
Importing tech isn't too hard, but the downsides may not be worth it.
There are many reasons to import phones or other tech, whether you're buying it in person during a trip or via online marketplaces or importers. Your phone could die while you're travelling abroad, for example, forcing you to buy a replacement. Or maybe there's a perfect product for you, but it's not available where you live. Either way, buying tech from other countries is sometimes the only option.
Depending on the product, though, this can come with a catch or two. Buying devices from other regions can come with annoying restrictions. You might end up with slightly different hardware, lack warranty coverage or, in the worst case, not have access to core software or connectivity features. Here's what you should know before buying a new phone, laptop or any other tech product from overseas.
Not every device is built to work globally
A device can have different hardware configurations globally. In China, for example, certain iPhone models have slots for two physical SIMs. Conversely, US iPhones dropped the SIM tray starting with the iPhone 14, so you must use an eSIM instead. iPhones sold in China also get limited access to Apple Intelligence tools, even if you use it elsewhere.
Phones may pose issues with cellular bands. Manufacturers usually offer different versions of the same phone designed for specific bands in a given region. If you buy a phone in another country, it might not work on the US' 5G network, for example. This means you could lose access to carrier-specific features like VoLTE or Wi-Fi Calling if the device you're buying isn't certified for your network. It may seem minor, but it can be a headache if you plan to use it as your main device.
Other tech isn't free from potential issues, either. Laptops, for instance, can have different keyboard layouts depending on where you buy them. French laptops will use the AZERTY layout, and not every brand offers a QWERTY version in such markets. Depending on the product, power can be an issue too: imported products will likely use a different plug, so you'll need an adaptor, but that's not all. Watch out for voltages as well; the US uses 120V at 60Hz, but most of Europe and Asia use 220V to 240V, usually at 50Hz. Phone and laptop chargers usually work worldwide, but not all tech will.
Limited warranty and duties
Warranty is also an issue depending on what you're buying. Many manufacturers only provide tech support in the region where the device was sold. And if you're buying a product that isn't officially sold in the US, getting a broken part repaired can be tough, too. Some companies are more flexible when it comes to supporting devices purchased abroad, as is the case with AppleCare. Still, the company's warranty terms state that it may limit service for select devices, including the iPhone, to the country where the product was originally sold. Buying locally is still a safer bet if warranty is a priority.
If you're buying online, you also have to contend with import duties and shipping costs. The US has eliminated its $800 de minimis exemption for international parcels, so even small packages may get taxed quite heavily. International shipping isn't cheap, either. Most of the time, then, you have to really decide whether what you want to buy overseas is worth it.

articles.title: I Let Pangram Loose on My Gmail Inbox. Here’s How Much AI It Found
articles.text:
AI-generated content is everywhere now: From restaurant menus and student essays to full-length movies and social media posts, AI is churning out huge amounts of text, images, audio, and video. In some digital spaces, it's overwhelming human-made content.
But what about your inbox? Just how many of your friends, family members, clients, and colleagues are using AI to compose their emails? Is that store newsletter you just signed up for written by a real person or a bot? It's not always easy to tell.
The Pangram AI text and image detector tool has now extended its reach into your Gmail inbox. The company makes a browser extension that sits in Gmail and runs incoming messages through its algorithms to try to detect AI writing.
You will need at least the $20-per-month individual plan on Pangram to use the Gmail integration—it's not available on the free tier. I tested it to see how accurate it appears to be based on my recent Gmail conversations.
Setting Up Pangram in Gmail
You can let Pangram loose in your Gmail inbox by heading to the Gmail integration page and clicking Connect your Gmail. You can also click the Gmail Integration entry on the left-hand navigation pane in your main Pangram dashboard on the web. You'll need to go through the standard authorization screens to confirm you want to make the connection.
Pangram says the contents of your emails aren't stored after being assessed and won't be used to train models designed to look for AI text. There's still a level of trust here, but you can quickly remove the Pangram plug-in from your Gmail at any point.
After you connect your Gmail account, Pangram gets to work. It'll scan your 100 most recent email threads and then any new messages from then on—you can't get it to check all of the emails you've ever received. As far as I can tell, email scanning doesn't count against your scan credit limit for the month, so you're covered no matter how busy your inbox is.
After scanning, the Gmail Integration part of your Pangram dashboard changes. You can see at a glance how many of your emails are suspected to be AI, how many are most probably human, and how many have been flagged as a mix between the two. Inside Gmail, these three categories can be applied as labels, though this is optional. (If you decide to remove Pangram from your inbox later, any labels it's created will stick around, but you can delete these manually.)
You can also choose to send incoming AI-written emails straight to the archive or to spam if you want, which is handy for keeping AI content away from your eyeballs. You can also choose to exclude specific domains, Gmail labels, subject keywords, and senders from Pangram's scans, if you don't want emails from your boss or mom scrutinized.
Scanning My Inbox With Pangram
So the moment of truth: Out of the 108 threads that Pangram scanned, eight of them were labeled as AI, 37 got the human label, and the remainder were marked as mixed. It's a little dispiriting to discover that way more than half of my incoming messages are probably AI-written, with press releases the most common culprits.
In terms of accuracy, none of the emails I know to have been written by flesh-and-blood people were flagged as fully or partly AI. Everything from friends and family and colleagues I know passed the human test, so for this small sample size at least, Pangram's detection algorithms seem to be working.
I sent a couple of emails to myself from different accounts to see what Pangram would make of them. One was written with Microsoft Copilot, which the detector correctly flagged as AI. The other was a section of this article, written with my own brain and keyboard taps, and again Pangram got it right—it was marked with the Human label.
There does seem to be a minimum email length, and if an email’s word count falls below that threshold, Pangram won't make a decision either way, which is understandable. (AI is harder to detect with a smaller sample size). Only the first email in each thread is scanned (and optionally labeled), so if your correspondent switches to AI halfway through a conversation, it wouldn't get spotted.
I like the way the scanner stays in the background and just gets on with its job, and I can see myself using it long-term. It really does affect your mindset if you know a message has been entirely put together using AI. Of course, Gmail being Gmail, you can quickly fire off an AI response as well, should you want to.
