articles.title: Medium's new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Online publishing platform Medium on Monday launched a new app, called TK, which aims to bring AI technology deeper into the writing process. The idea behind TK is to make it easier to turn ideas into written words by incorporating an AI assistant into the editor itself, allowing users to ask for help by typing “@TK” followed by their request or prompt.
In publishing and journalism, the term “TK” serves as a placeholder used to mark where missing information can be added later. The “TK” stands for “to come,” but uses a “K” instead of “C” as there are few English words where the “tk” letter combination exists, making it stand out more easily in written text where it could be caught by proofreaders.
In Medium’s app, TK takes on a new role as it tries to help users fill in the blanks.
The company suggests the AI assistant could help answer questions that you might normally have to switch to another tab to quickly look up, like how many days are in a particular month. The app could also pull in bits of writing you had previously saved to the app when you were still fleshing out your ideas.
In addition, Medium says TK will ship with particular skills for editorial feedback, headline feedback, and others that could match your draft to the style guide for Medium publications.
Medium’s move to embrace AI in the early stages of writing could prove controversial at a time when the publishing and literary worlds have been reckoning with the role that artificial intelligence has played in the creation of new long-form prose. Multiple authors have lost book deals over suspicions that they used AI technology to help them write, while other literary awards have come under scrutiny after winners were suspected of writing with AI assistance.
While writers have long used automated tools for proofreading and light grammatical edits, there is growing concern across the publishing industry that an AI assistant’s editorial “suggestions” can become the writing itself, instead of being reflective of the thoughts in the writer’s own mind.
But because AI models were trained on human writing, there are also questions around the reliability of AI detection tools in terms of their ability to properly determine when something was written with AI, rather than with its assistance, versus not at all.
TK leans into this debate, taking the side that these nuances will ultimately no longer matter in the end. Instead, the company celebrates what AI can bring to the world of writing, saying that “artificial intelligence makes writing more important, not less,” and proclaiming that “AI is a technology that has the power to amplify human intelligence and it uses the written word as a foundation.”
Still, Medium concedes that AI does raise the possibility of low-quality content and blurring the line between what’s human-written versus AI-written. To address these concerns, TK allows authors to publish notes that transparently explain how AI was used in their writing.
“This is a start of what we believe is required to publish in the AI era, which is to make the provenance of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, right down to the prompting and source material,” Medium explained in a blog post about the launch.
In addition to writing assistance, TK will help users remember and organize what they had previously written and suggest writing prompts. The app can also optionally connect to your own AI agent through TK’s MCP server or Claude skill, so the app can better understand your projects, your positions, and other ideas that could be stored in your agent’s memory.
Meanwhile, the new app incorporates human feedback in a social layer, the company says, allowing writers to share their early drafts with others and get feedback.
At launch, TK is available on the web, but a desktop app is on the roadmap, Medium says. The app can import and export Markdown, but it’s not a Markdown app itself. The writing in TK is also not encrypted, as the app is designed for collaboration, but users will be able to set access control permissions on their work.
Medium, which is profitable, says TK will be a free tool for those with a Medium account.

articles.title: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
articles.text:
After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”
Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence.
These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.
For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

articles.title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
articles.text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.
To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.
The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.
Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.
Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.
Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.
In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.
That, however, has changed. The Trump administration recently argued in court that because the Customs Service’s powers were transferred to DHS following the passing of the Homeland Security Act, it can use that power to tackle its “broad investigative portfolio,” which it says includes enforcing laws “beyond legacy customs and immigration enforcement.”
“When we give law enforcement agencies powerful investigative tools, even with the best intentions and purposes to try to go after legitimate investigations and crime, you have to be really careful,” says Mackey. The newly reported filing is part of an ongoing Freedom of Information Act lawsuit filed by the nonprofit against ICE and DHS.
"The numbers reported to EFF amount to a dragnet domestic surveillance program by Trump's Homeland Security Department,” says US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon.
ICE did not respond to questions about why there’s been such a huge increase compared to prior years, but Mackey speculates that it may be because there is virtually no downside to filing them.
“The worst thing that will happen to ICE is that the service that receives it says it's not going to respond,” says Mackey. If that happens, ICE can just take the company to court to force it to comply, as it recently did with Google, or withdraw it and try to get the information it’s after by issuing a grand jury subpoena, as the Intercept reported it recently did with Reddit.
“Congress desperately needs to pass my bipartisan legislation to drastically curb federal subpoenas, including consequences for officials who abuse surveillance authorities,” says Wyden, referencing his proposed Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act. “Next year, I plan to use the Senate Finance Committee gavel to get to the bottom of HSI's unprecedented misuse of customs law to target Trump's enemies.”
Even without exact details about the 185,000 subpoenas HSI sent out, Mackey says their prolific uses still raises “significant concerns about an agency potentially being out of control and not being subject to any sort of internal oversight that respects people's First Amendment rights and their rights to privacy.”

articles.title: Meta expands Instagram's AI age-guessing tech globally | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta announced on Monday that it’s expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology on Instagram worldwide to identify more teens and place them under its Teen Account protections, as it faces numerous lawsuits accusing its platforms of harming teens.
The social media giant says it will use the AI technology to find people it suspects to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday.
Teen Accounts place users into a stricter account experience with additional safeguards, such as receiving direct messages only from people they follow or are already connected to, hiding harmful comments, and setting accounts to private by default.
Meta’s age-guessing tools use AI to analyze entire profiles for contextual clues, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades. Meta also looks for these signals across different formats, such as posts, comments, bios, captions, and more. The company also looks at visual cues from photos and videos, including a person’s height or bone structure.
Meta said it’s continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, with a similar global rollout planned for Threads later this year.
The global expansion comes as Meta reached settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August to resolve lawsuits alleging its platforms harm teens. As part of the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
“We’ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps,” Meta wrote in a blog post. “That’s why as part of our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may belong to teens between the ages of 13 and 17 so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday.”
Meta said parents in the U.S. will start seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining its approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections.

articles.title: Hai ngân hàng lớn vượt qua Big4 về tăng dư nợ, lộ diện 6 nhà băng bơm tiền mạnh nhất
articles.text:
VPBank và MB dẫn đầu về mức tăng cho vay khách hàng
Thống kê tại 30 ngân hàng thương mại trong nước (ngoại trừ SCB và 4 ngân hàng chuyển giao bắt buộc), số dư cho vay khách hàng tại thời điểm 30/9/2026 đạt 17,471 triệu tỷ đồng, tăng 1,751 triệu tỷ đồng, tương đương 11,13% so với đầu năm.
Điều bất ngờ là không phải nhóm ngân hàng Big4, mà VPBank và MB là hai ngân hàng thương mại cổ phần có mức tăng dư nợ cho vay khách hàng lớn nhất trong nhóm ngân hàng được khảo sát (xét theo giá trị tuyệt đối) trong 9 tháng qua.
Cụ thể, VPBank với 252.344 tỷ đồng dư nợ tăng thêm so với đầu năm, qua đó đạt mức tăng trưởng tín dụng hơn 30%. Đáng chú ý, đây là lần đầu tiên VPBank đạt dư nợ cho vay vượt 1 triệu tỷ đồng, khi dư nợ cho vay khách hàng tính đến 30/9 là 1,085 triệu tỷ đồng.
Trong khi đó, dư nợ cho vay khách hàng đến 30/9 của Ngân hàng MB tăng 196.000 tỷ đồng so với đầu năm, đạt 1,215 triệu tỷ đồng.
Nhóm các ngân hàng ghi nhận dư nợ cho vay tăng thêm vượt 100.000 tỷ đồng trong 9 tháng đầu năm còn có: BIDV tăng thêm 186.000 tỷ, Agribank tăng thêm 170.000 tỷ, HDBank tăng thêm 154.000 tỷ, VietinBank tăng thêm 141.000 tỷ.
Xét về tỷ lệ tăng trưởng cho vay, NCB dẫn đầu với mức tăng trưởng tín dụng đạt 54,5%, PVcomBank tăng 30,4%, VPBank tăng 30,29%, HDBank tăng 29,81%, LPBank tăng 23%...
Nhóm Big4 nắm 47% thị phần cho vay
Nhóm ngân hàng thương mại nhà nước (Big4) dù dẫn đầu toàn ngành về dư nợ cho vay khách hàng nhưng vẫn cho thấy sự thận trọng khi chỉ ghi nhận tăng trưởng tín dụng thấp hơn mức bình quân toàn ngành.
Cụ thể, Agribank đạt mức tăng trưởng tín dụng 8,8% so với đầu năm, ghi dấu mốc đáng nhớ khi lần đầu tiên “ông lớn” này đạt mức dư nợ cho vay khách hàng vượt ngưỡng 2 triệu tỷ đồng (cụ thể là 2,106 triệu tỷ đồng).
BIDV tiếp tục khẳng định ngôi vị số 1 về lượng vốn bơm ra cho nền kinh tế khi dư nợ cho vay khách hàng đạt hơn 2,47 triệu tỷ đồng, tăng 8,14% so với đầu năm.
Với 2,082 triệu tỷ đồng dư nợ cho vay khách hàng đến 30/9, VietinBank đạt mức tăng trưởng tín dụng 7,28% so với đầu năm, đồng thời cũng đánh dấu lần đầu tiên trong lịch sử đạt mốc dư nợ cho vay khách hàng vượt 2 triệu tỷ đồng.
Trong khi đó, Vietcombank gần như không có sự thay đổi nào về cho vay khách hàng so với đầu năm, với tổng dư nợ đến 30/9 đạt 1,629 triệu tỷ đồng.
Bên cạnh đó, hai ngân hàng ghi nhận mức tăng trưởng tín dụng âm trong ba quý đầu năm là Saigonbank giảm 0,98%, đạt 21.520 tỷ; Eximbank giảm 17,42% với mức dư nợ cho vay là 150.221 tỷ đồng.
Như vậy, kết thúc ba quý đầu năm, có 6 ngân hàng đạt số dư cho vay khách hàng vượt 1 triệu tỷ đồng, gồm nhóm Big4 và MB, VPBank.
Trong đó, tổng dư nợ cho vay khách hàng của nhóm Big4 đạt 8,29 triệu tỷ đồng, tương đương khoảng 47,5% tổng dư nợ của nhóm.
BIDV tiếp tục dẫn đầu về thị phần cho vay, lên tới 14%. Thị phần cho vay của VietinBank và Agribank cùng đạt 12%, trong khi thị phần của Vietcombank là 9%.

articles.title: Those white cameras mounted above traffic lights serve a little-known purpose - Engadget
articles.text:
Those white cameras mounted above traffic lights serve a little-known purpose
Unlike Flock cameras, they're only meant to keep traffic flowing.
Automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) are nothing new, but reported abuses have made drivers understandably wary of the cameras made by Flock and other companies, to the point of wanting to find out where they are so they can be avoided. While that added attention has made intersection cameras seem more visible than ever, not every camera you see mounted above the road serves the same purpose. Most cameras on roadways aren't used to track individual drivers, but rather to monitor traffic conditions.
Aside from ALPRs, cameras meant to track people running red lights are also controversial. They're banned in many states, and they're rare even where they're allowed. Far more common are cameras used to monitor traffic conditions in real time or automatically control traffic lights.
Most cameras are there to control the flow of traffic
Distinct from cameras used to catch drivers speeding or running red lights, traffic cameras aren't designed to capture evidence for law enforcement. Instead, they're meant to be watched live to monitor the current state of traffic and keep an eye out for accidents. This real-time data can be used by local transportation departments to help keep traffic moving, by overriding automatic light timings in some cases, or to alert first responders when needed. These systems can also be used to track traffic patterns over time, helping traffic engineers determine when changes need to be made to roadways or signals to control congestion.
In many cases, the cameras mounted on traffic lights are tied to automatic signaling systems rather than providing a live video feed. These cameras send data to control systems that determine when lights should cycle. Engineers can designate a section of the video frame that the camera should monitor for the presence of cars. When a car enters that space, it triggers the light to change based on a timing sequence that pre-programmed for each individual roadway. In addition to video cameras, these systems often use radar, infrared cameras and electromagnetic detectors built into roads to detect the presence of vehicles.
Exactly what the cameras on roadways are used for varies widely based on where they are. Local laws determine which types of cameras are allowed to be installed in the first place, and how they're used depends on the needs of a particular intersection. While there's plenty of justified concern over the prevalence of Flock cameras and other ALPRs, chances are when you see a camera mounted above a traffic light, it's just there to keep things moving.

articles.title: Apple’s CEO presses Federighi to move faster toward an agentic Siri
articles.text:
Apple chief executive John Ternus has pushed software chief Craig Federighi to speed up Apple’s AI plans, Mark Gurman reported for Bloomberg on Sunday. Ternus wants Apple to move beyond improving Siri. According to the report, he held a closed-door meeting with Federighi in recent weeks. Ternus is frustrated by what he sees as Apple’s reluctance to match its rivals’ urgency on AI. TNW has not independently verified the report.
In public, Ternus has struck a different tone. On Apple’s earnings call last week, he praised the new Siri AI. Last month he told WIRED that Apple would not ship AI for AI’s sake.
“It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time,” Ternus said on the call. “As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users.”
An AI sceptic in charge of Apple’s AI
Federighi became Apple’s AI chief last year, after the company removed its former AI leader, John Giannandrea. He still has a reputation as an AI sceptic, Gurman wrote. He has worried about the technology’s effects on privacy, security, society and jobs.
Some employees describe a hands-on management style that leaves little room for competing ideas, according to Bloomberg. Federighi also tends to plan over 12 to 18 months, while Apple’s hardware teams work to multiyear road maps.
He also led the rebuild that brought a working Siri AI to market with iOS 27. The new Siri runs on models based on technology Apple licenses from Google.
Mike Rockwell, Apple’s vice president of Siri engineering, is still seriously considering stepping down next year, Bloomberg reported. He could leave the role or Apple altogether. More responsibility would then likely fall to two people. One is Amar Subramanya, a Google veteran Apple hired last year. The other is Sebastien Marineau, a Federighi deputy. Some inside Apple see Marineau as a possible future successor to Federighi.
From in-app actions to an agentic Siri
The iOS 27.3 beta lets Siri carry out precise actions inside Apple’s own apps. It can organise Safari tabs, sort folders in Files and unsend an iMessage. It can also edit and share a photo in several steps. Gurman expects that to reach users as early as December, with the public release of iOS 27.3.
Support for third-party apps will probably follow in the spring, with iOS 27.5 or iOS 27.6, he wrote. That would let Siri book a table through OpenTable or place an order through Uber Eats.
Even then, Siri would only act when asked. OpenAI’s ChatGPT Dots, Meta’s Muse and Grok can take on ongoing tasks, track goals and keep working between conversations.
“Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year,” Gurman wrote.
Apple also lacks a computer-use tool, Gurman noted. ChatGPT and Claude already offer one, which can read a screen, move a cursor, click buttons and type into apps.
A new schedule for iOS 28
Apple has also changed how it builds next year’s operating systems, according to Bloomberg. Each development milestone normally splits into four weeks of coding and four weeks of integrating features into the system.
The first milestone for iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28 gave engineers six weeks of coding and two of integration. Employees say they like the change, Gurman reported. Work on the second milestone, when Apple starts to finalise features, begins on Monday.

articles.title: Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models
articles.text:
Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.
Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models
Claude Fable 5.2 is designed to take on big technical challenges, and it’s available today.
Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems.
During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.
Claude Fable 5.2 is launching today. As for Claude Mythos 5.2, only vetted organizations will have access to start. The new 5.2 models follow the release of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in September.

articles.title: Waymo robotaxis kept illegally passing school buses after software fix, feds say | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nearly a year ago, Waymo updated its self-driving software and issued a recall after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses that had stopped and deployed flashing red lights. Now, federal safety regulators have opened a new investigation into why that behavior has continued.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said in a November 6 filing that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem.
Reuters was the first to report the filing.
Waymo said last year that a software update was completed for all affected vehicles on November 17, 2025. However, NHTSA said the majority of the incidents occurred after the software update. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) has opened a “recall query” to “assess the adequacy of the remedy.”
The ODI opened its initial investigation into Waymo in October 2025 after seeing footage of one of its autonomous vehicles maneuvering around a stopped school bus that had its stop sign extended, lights flashing, and was unloading children in Atlanta. In that incident, a Waymo robotaxi crossed perpendicularly in front of the school bus from its right side. The autonomous vehicle then turned left around the front of the bus before traveling down the street.
Numerous other incidents have been documented in the weeks and months since in Austin, where Waymo also operates a robotaxi service. Austin Independent School District officials reported at least five such incidents at the time, according to a letter filed with NHTSA.
Reached for comment, Waymo stressed the importance of safety to its mission. “We have made significant improvements to vehicle behavior around school buses and have received no citations since March 2026,” a spokesperson told TechCrunch via email. “The Waymo Driver has a clearly demonstrated positive impact on roadway safety. Once received, we’ll work to respond to NHTSA’s query and look forward to continuing our engagement on recall processes for AV software that continues to learn and improve.”
TechCrunch also reached out to Austin Independent School District officials for comment and will update the article if they respond.
This article was updated after publication with Waymo’s statement.

articles.title: Bikers and Bug-Lovers Join Forces to Fight a New Google Data Center
articles.text:
On Wednesday afternoon, Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London.
Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site.
Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility.
Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them, hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US, people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works.
Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour. Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week. In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner.
“There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.”
The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake.
Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.)
The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget.
“We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.”
Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030. Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.”
Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.”
There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London.
Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step.
“These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”

articles.title: Google lets developers add Maps to AI Studio apps for free
articles.text:
Google AI Studio can now set up Google Maps Platform for apps built by prompting Gemini, with a free demo key allowing 100 calls a day per API. Production apps still need a paid Cloud billing account, but the same key and code keep working.
Developers can now add Google Maps to apps they build in Google AI Studio without leaving it, Google said on Monday. AI Studio sets up the maps service and its key on its own, and no credit card is needed to start.
Users describe an app to Gemini, and AI Studio connects Google Maps Platform and loads a live map preview. Google’s example is a request for “an interactive 3D tour of NYC showcasing iconic landmarks.”
The free demo key allows 100 calls a day for each Maps API, resetting every 24 hours, Google’s developer blog says. Apps can use maps, place search, routes, and local data such as pollen and air quality. One sample app plans routes for a pet grooming van around fixed appointments.
There are limits. For people new to Google Cloud, the demo key covers most Maps APIs but not route optimisation, solar data or Nav Connect. Existing Cloud users get a smaller set without photos and reviews from users, Google’s documentation shows.
To launch an app, developers must add a paid billing account, which brings standard Maps pricing. The same key keeps working, so the code doesn’t change.
The free key itself isn’t new. Google launched its no-credit-card Maps Demo Key in November 2025. What’s new is that AI Studio now creates and connects it automatically.
Google has been turning AI Studio into a place where anyone can build apps by prompting. Since October, people can publish AI Studio apps to the Play Store for free, and developers can move projects to Antigravity, its agent coding tool. Apple has gone the other way, cracking down on AI-built apps.

articles.title: You can grab three months of Game Pass Ultimate for under $20 per month
articles.text:
The price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate has fluctuated between $20 and $30 per month over the last year, but you can get three months of the top plan for around $19 per month. At Newegg, using the coupon code BNWF2656 at checkout knocks $11 off the usual cost of a three-month subscription. That brings the price down to just $57.99 for three months. In addition to full access to over 500 games on both Xbox consoles and Windows PC machines, the upgraded Ultimate plan includes EA Play and Ubisoft Plus Classics, which have their own libraries and benefits, and Fortnite Crew for full access to the Fortnite battles passes. On Xbox, Ultimate enables online multiplayer, as well.
You can grab three months of Game Pass Ultimate for under $20 per month
We also spotted discounts on a capable Ryzen 7 CPU, the Lego Pokémon Pikachu set, and a Bose soundbar.
Previously a straightforward proposition, the service has undergone a variety of changes over the last year that has made it slightly less appealing. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate was previously $29.99 per month, but earlier this year Microsoft removed the Call of Duty games from the library, and in the process dropped the price to $22.99.
More recently, Microsoft added hourly limits to cloud gaming. All Game Pass plan subscribers previously enjoyed an unlimited amount of cloud gaming on their computer or mobile device, but now plans scale the number of included hours, with the Ultimate plan including 15 hours per month. That news came just weeks before announcing pay-as-you-go plans for non-Game Pass subscribers.
Other deals to consider
- The AMD Ryzen 7 9700X is discounted to $269 at various retailers, including Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H, a $70 break from the usual price. This eight-core, 16-thread desktop CPU is compatible with AM5 motherboards, and has a maximum boost clock of up to 5.5GHz out of the box, with full support for overclocking. It’s probably overkill for light gaming, but serious gamers and demanding PC users will get the a lot of bang for their buck with this AMD processor. The discounted price lets you reach near AMD’s fastest consumer chip offerings, and is much cheaper than the faster Ryzen 7 9800X3D.
- This Lego Pokémon Pikachu and Pokéball set is on sale for $159.95 at Amazon. That $40 discount is the largest we’ve seen since the collaboration launched back in March, and a remarkably good value for a set with 2,050 pieces. Once built, it’s a sizable set, standing 13.5 inches tall and 15.5 inches deep, and the Pikachu has posable ears and limbs. This seems like a fantastic gift, either to yourself or to another Pokémon fan you care about.
- Amazon has the Bose Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar marked down to $899, a $200 discount from the usual price. This Dolby Atmos-equipped soundbar supports eARC over HDMI, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for easy adjustments or listening to music, and has Alexa voice commands for when you can’t find the remote. You can also combine the soundbar with Bose Lifestyle Ultra Speakers for a proper surround system.

articles.title: Meet Drops, the new music app bringing back the fun of sharing songs with friends | TechCrunch
articles.text:
There’s a new music discovery app borrowing the endless vertical-scrolling format of TikTok. But instead of watching videos, users swipe through short clips of songs, hoping to stumble upon their next favorite artist.
Launched Monday by Harman, a Samsung subsidiary, Drops aims to make discovering new music feel social again.
Available on iOS and Android in the U.S., the app lets users scroll through 10- to 30-second snippets of songs, accompanied by lyrics, album artwork, artist photos, and captions. The idea is to give listeners just enough of a track to grab their attention, whether it’s a particularly good lyric, a catchy hook, or a beat that makes them want to hear more.
The company says Drops is meant to feel like a return to how people used to discover music in the first place. Before every platform’s algorithm recommendations, people often heard about new songs through friends, music blogs, or online communities. Drops is trying to recreate that experience.
“You send a friend a song and say, ‘You have to hear this.’ Then you end up texting, ‘Skip to 1:47, that’s the best part.’ The part that hits usually isn’t the first few seconds, and there wasn’t a good way to share just that moment,” Clare Hunter, general manager of Drops, told us.
Hunter explained that the idea for Drops began taking shape after Harman acquired music management software company Roon in 2023.
“I used to spend hours making mixtapes for my friends, picking the songs, the order, and decorating the cover. Drops is the version of that I always wanted,” Hunter added.
The app is easy to navigate, with tabs including “For You,” “New,” “Showcase,” and “Following,” along with relevant and trending hashtags.
Users can like, comment, repost, share, and save tracks to collections called Droplists. They can also send songs directly to other users, follow other profiles, and exchange direct messages.
To listen to the entire track, Drops offers integrations with major streaming services, including Apple Music, Qobuz, and TIDAL. Users can jump directly into the full version of the song through their connected streaming platform.
Notably, the company says it doesn’t use generative AI for audio or visuals. Songs appear as they were originally released, using official album artwork and licensed artist photography. At a time when AI-generated music and slop are becoming harder to avoid, this will likely appeal to many users.
Another part worth noting is that Drops pays rights holders and reports plays back to its partners. Those partners include Universal Music Group, Beggars Group, Empire, Symphonic Distribution, and UnitedMasters.
Plays also count toward streams on those services, meaning Drops isn’t trying to replace existing music subscriptions.
Drops is currently invite-only, with U.S. users able to join the waitlist.

articles.title: Welcome to Weed Island
articles.text:
Steven Tan walks along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones.
But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.”
Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification.
Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy.
Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”
Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says.
The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing.
Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says.
Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich.
Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor.
Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO. That year, it was valued at just £3.7 million, despite having spent as much as £30 million on its weed-growing facility.
Tan nevertheless saw a lot of potential, and over the last two years has seen capacity at the site increase from 25 percent to 75 percent. He believes the £8.4 million of product the company exported last year is just the beginning.
Sarah Clover, a barrister at Kings Chambers who works on cannabis licensing in Jersey, told WIRED the island’s advantage is hard to replicate. Growers are inspected by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is known for enforcing rigorous standards on quality. “Anybody buying from Jersey knows that the stuff coming out of it is absolutely gold standard, because the MHRA says it is,” she says. Permits, however, are handled by a small team on the island: “You can make an application for a permit on a Monday and get it on a Tuesday.”
Many within the Jersey medicinal cannabis industry now want to go beyond growing the raw ingredient and package it for export as a final product on the island. Northern Leaf already has the facilities to do so, but Jersey law dictates it can only export bulk amounts of raw cannabis for other companies to process and pack for distribution and sale. The company is waiting to see if Jersey will change its law. “At the minute we’re kind of on this seesaw—which way will the island go?” Clover says. “It could really take off here. Jersey could be a life sciences hub, not just for cannabis but for all sorts of pharmaceuticals.”
But running a cannabis business on a small island poses challenges, and not everyone is enthused about the idea of expansion. Tan has faced off against residents every time that the facility has expanded production. Some locals have complained that they can smell cannabis from their balconies. Others have linked the growing industry to concerns over misuse of cannabis on the island, despite the fact that all of its product is exported. Cannabis is a “contributory factor” in 22 percent of admissions to the island’s acute mental health ward, according to Jersey’s health minister.
One patient, Michael, told WIRED that he was prescribed medical cannabis for 18 months after having tried two other prescribed medications for insomnia and anxiety. “The initial assessment was simple. I had a meeting with the cannabis doctor who was pretty evangelical about its medicinal properties. They check your medical history with your GP, and within 10 days you’re good to go,” he says.
Michael was prescribed 30 grams a month of “unbelievably good” cannabis and told that if he ran out he could back and ask for more. “I stopped because it was seriously affecting my mental health [and] I have since seen a psychiatric professional who said I should never have been prescribed it given my documented mental health history,” he says.
Illegal resale of medical cannabis is also an issue, with a rise in so-called “user-dealers,” who sell their excess medical marijuana to others. Jersey Police told WIRED this “undermines the legal framework and creates opportunities for criminal supply.”
Overall, however, cannabis-related offenses have dropped since Jersey legalized medical cannabis in 2019—from 216 in 2016 to just 12, as of July 2026.
Tan is circumspect about the challenges of operating on Jersey. “Culturally, the people here are harder to convince about cannabis,” he says. “It’s an older society.” But after 25 years working in the industry, he’s used to the pushback.
“It’s a normal challenge,” he says. “And I think when anyone sits down and meets me, they understand. This isn’t a bunch of stoners growing a bit of weed in a plastic greenhouse.”
While Jersey’s medical cannabis industry grows, some people on the island want to go further. In 2024, a vote to decriminalize recreational cannabis was defeated by a single vote in the island’s parliament. When it was brought back for another vote by the island’s then health minister, it was withdrawn before it could be debated. It is expected to be brought back before the parliament in the coming months.
Some individuals on the island have decided not to wait. By exploiting a loophole in current laws, they have made Jersey one of the only places in Europe outside of Amsterdam where THC products can be purchased and consumed legally.
One morning in February 2024, Gary Tucker arrived at work, his weed shop in St Helier, Jersey, to find a dozen customs officers and the local media waiting outside. It was a raid—and not his first. The officers emptied shelves and boxes into bin bags. “They were literally running their arms down the shelves and putting everything into bags. They took everything,” Tucker, a California native and former analyst in the US Army, told WIRED.
Tucker operates outside of Jersey’s medical cannabis industry. His shop, Bailiwick Botanicals, sells products that are clearly recreational: hash cakes, gummies, and other snacks, all infused with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis that gets you high and is heavily controlled.
He’s able to do this owing to a loophole in Jersey law which allows the sale of products containing CBD—another critical ingredient in cannabis, but one that doesn’t get you high. Jersey’s law says that the amount of THC in CBD products cannot exceed 3 percent of the weight of the CBD. So, if you want to sell products with high levels of THC, you just have to boost the CBD. “It’s just a math equation,” Tucker says.
Tucker admits it isn’t an ideal situation: studies suggest that ingesting high levels of CBD can cause liver damage. But he sees that as an issue with the regulation, not his solution. “I’m just following consumer demand,” he says.
Tucker is somewhat evangelical about the properties of cannabis. In his time as a weapons trainer for the military, he struggled with the mental health impacts of hearing that recruits he had trained had been killed in action. “I needed to step back from it. It started to really affect my mind,” Tucker says.
Veterans he knew were turning to cannabis, and Tucker began buying it on the black market. “It was the only thing that helped me,” he says. ”Cannabis gave me my life back.”
Tucker currently manufactures most of his products in the US before shipping them to Sark—a smaller Channel Island best known for having no cars and also its own government—and then to Jersey. New regulations in the US, however, mean Tucker may need to change his approach.
Tucker sees Jersey as a potential export hub for THC products to Europe. He believes Jersey’s budding weed industry should push beyond medical cannabis and into the recreational market. “This isn’t just a bunch of guys in a cellar somewhere. Not only does cannabis help people, but getting it to the shelf creates jobs. From the grower to the retailer. It permeates across all industries. We’re making cosmetics. We’re making gummies. We’re making drinks,” he says.
After the 2024 raid, Bailiwick Botanicals shut its doors for two weeks, and its full stock wasn’t returned until six months later. As of June 2026, Tucker and his team are selling THC-infused fudge, chocolate, and other sweets. His newest product, THC-infused coffee beans, is selling well. The police have stayed away.
In a written statement to WIRED, Jersey’s government said that the “possibility of abuse of our limits to get round the law in other jurisdictions is a matter of concern to the Government of Jersey and we are looking at ways to address it. Work is underway to consider whether Jersey’s existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.”
For his part, Tan is reluctant to be drawn on his views on the so-called “rec” (recreational) market. For now, Jersey still has harsh sentencing rules on recreational cannabis use, with the penalties for possession and possession with intent to supply remaining up to five years and 14 years in jail, respectively. The proposed (and withdrawn) law to decriminalize cannabis notes that, the way the law is currently written, someone who rolled three joints and gave one to a friend would be guilty of supply and receive a criminal record. “Without change, people will continue receiving serious criminal records for small amounts … punishments [that] can result in additional harms greater than the drug itself,” it said.
While Jersey makes its own laws, however, it may not be able to completely legalize cannabis. Jersey is a signatory to the UN Convention on drugs control via the UK, and the UK Home Office would undoubtedly have a view if the island were to set itself up as an “Amsterdam on the Sea.” In 2022, an effort by the government of Bermuda (a British Overseas Territory) to legalize recreational cannabis was blocked after the UK withheld Royal Assent from the bill.
Back at the Northern Leaf warehouse in the Jersey parish of St Lawrence, Tan is flipping the lids off large boxes and rifling through clear plastic bags packed full of cannabis.
This is all weed that will not be sold, either because there were issues with production or the THC levels were too low. Instead, it is taken to a secure area of the facility where it is locked away in a reinforced armored vault. Specialist staff with bodycams take the bags to the island’s incinerator, where it is unceremoniously burned, as required by law.
Tan regularly makes a case to the government for changes to the law and support for the cannabis industry, such as an industrial energy tariff to help with spiraling energy costs.
He has claimed that Jersey could be home to “the Monsanto of cannabis,” alluding to the agricultural giant that was acquired by pharmaceutical company Bayer in 2018 for $66 billion. He’d like to get deeper into the genetics of cannabis, form a tissue-culture lab, and “bring out strains that nobody has ever seen.”
But speaking of himself, he references a different genre of business: He’s Willy Wonka, but for weed. Thirty years ago, when Tan quit corporate finance, his father warned him that he could make a lot more money if he stayed in banking. “And you know what, he was right,” he says. “But I would not have had nearly as much fun.”

articles.title: Nominal’s $240M Series C triples its valuation to $3B in eight months
articles.text:
Nominal, whose software helps engineers test and analyse hardware such as aircraft, satellites and robots, has raised $240M in a Series C round at a $3B valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners led the round and Insight Partners co-led it, Nominal announced on Monday.
That is triple its valuation in March. Back then, Nominal raised $80M at $1B in a round led by Founders Fund. Nominal told Paayal Zaveri at Bloomberg that its revenue has more than tripled so far this year. Bloomberg linked that growth to a boom in defence technology spending.
Lux Capital, Sequoia, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, Avenir, Salesforce Ventures, M13 and Lockheed Martin Ventures also invested in Nominal’s Series C. So did Red Glass Ventures, PSP Growth and Deployment Capital.
“Hardware engineering is getting its AI moment, with real operational value that goes far beyond making existing workflows faster,” said Cameron McCord, Nominal’s co-founder and chief executive. “The companies building the world’s most advanced machines have decades of hard-won knowledge in their organizations.”
Five of the seven largest defence contractors
More than 80 commercial and government organisations use Nominal, including five of the seven largest defence contractors, the company says. Its software brings together test data from hardware and the engineering context behind it, such as configurations and earlier experiments. Nominal Analyst, its first AI agent, runs analyses on that data and traces its answers back to the evidence.
In a blog post on Monday, Nominal said better AI models alone will not produce better machines. A design can look right on paper and still fail once engineers build and test it.
“In engineering, physics gets a vote,” the company wrote.
Nominal gives three customer examples. At Anduril Industries, more than 300 engineers use it. Analysis that took five to six hours now happens in near real time. HII cut some analysis tasks from hours to minutes and some production test steps by about half.
Hypersonic aircraft maker Hermeus cut the time between uploading data and reviewing it by 80%. It designed and built its Quarterhorse Mk 1 aircraft in seven months.
The US Air Force recently selected Nominal for a $71.2M Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI). The money supports capability development for Collaborative Combat Aircraft, the uncrewed jets designed to fly alongside piloted fighters.
Agents, new industries and more acquisitions
Nominal will spend the new money on agents and applications across a machine’s whole life. They range from requirements checks and planning to scheduling and fleet health. It also plans to expand into new industries and regions, including through acquisitions.
This year it bought Fid Labs, whose team is building its agents. It also bought Pull Systems, which takes the platform into the car industry. Nominal announced the Pull Systems deal on 6 November.
Nominal started in 2022. Its headquarters are in Austin, and it has offices in Los Angeles, New York, Seattle, Washington, D.C. and London.
“Over the next five years, companies that effectively bring AI into their engineering workflows will have a real competitive advantage,” McCord said.

articles.title: Instagram’s Effect Builder makes new filters from AI prompts
articles.text:
After expanding its Edits app to macOS last week, Instagram’s next move is launching this Effect Builder that generates custom filters for your Stories posts with AI. Available now for US residents who are over 18, it has a prompt box for describing your filter idea to the chatbot, with an option to attach style reference images.
Instagram’s Effect Builder makes new filters from AI prompts
The Effect Builder bot is available on the web to build whatever new Instagram filters you can think of.
Then you can upload your own photos to preview the AI-generating effects, and ask for changes in follow-up prompts. There’s also an option to allow Instagram’s AI to rewrite your prompt, which turned my one-line test prompt “Make a filter that turns photos into comic book pages” into several AI-generated paragraphs of detailed style requests on everything from color palette to lighting. The filter Effect Builder generated as a result still looked nearly identical to its output for my original one-liner.
You can submit your filters to Instagram directly from Effect Builder, but effects have to pass a safety review before they’ll be available to other users. Instagram says after an effect is approved, it “shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.”

articles.title: Automattic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coding apps amid a changing internet | TechCrunch
articles.text:
WordPress has been a crucial technology and content management system for websites like TechCrunch. Now, WordPress.com owner Automattic is responding to the changing state of the web by debuting a new service called Spacefast, which will allow users to deploy vibe-coded websites and apps.
Spacefast is designed to provide infrastructure for the vibe-coded apps, including databases, authentication, file uploads, emails, and analytics, to make them functional websites, apps, or services. The product competes with the likes of Lovable and Emergent, which offer both interface and rails for vibe-coded apps, but in a more open way.
Users can connect Spacefast with other agents and chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, Grok Bot, Muse, Pi, Cursor, OpenCode, and Amp. Alternatively, they can connect a Git repository to Spacefast to get started.
The product is headed by Batuhan İçöz, who worked on it during one of the company’s hackathon sprints earlier in the year. At that time, he worked on the company’s cross-platform messaging app Beeper and said that he often got Vercel links from his non-technical friends while exploring vibe coding.
“I thought there had to be a better way for everyone to set up and deploy their projects. Automattic already has good infrastructure, but we have been traditionally associated with just WordPress. I thought, why do I have to use Cloudflare when we have a CDN (content delivery network) just as good? So I started working on what was called Stattic and now Spacefast,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
İçöz eventually disseminated the solution to his friends and added more features to make the product more dynamic. Automattic soft-launched the product in September to get feedback before today’s launch. 
The company has seen varied use cases of their product, with people and organizations using it for internal mockups, slideshows, and offer-related websites. However, that’s not the only competition Spacefast has. Productivity and design software like Figma, Canva, and Notion have launched products that sit at the intersection of vibe coding, mockups, and presentations.
İçöz thinks that, compared to something like Lovable, Spacefast has the advantage of giving users a choice of their agent and using the solution their way. The counter-argument might be that a certain kind of user wouldn’t want to choose and just have everything figured out for them.
Spacefast said that it also has the advantage of being within Automattic to launch solutions like web analytics, WordPress integration, and e-commerce features (through WooCommerce) easily to compete better with the whole lot.
“For enterprises, the problem right now is IT sprawl, as their marketing teams are churning out landing pages on services like Lovable, and they want to consolidate and work with a company that understands the enterprise needs. With our existing products, we have experience serving enterprise customers,” İçöz noted.
A challenge for newly minted products in the AI world is to retain people post-launch. Users might get excited to try out a new product, and then move on to the new shiny thing within days or weeks. İçöz is cognizant of the fact and said that he expects people to churn, as they might not be interested in making apps at all.
“I think what we need to do as a product is make sure that when you build something with SpaceFast, it is so easy, and the results are so much better than without Spacefast,” İçöz emphasized.
Many websites and publishers are struggling with dwindling traffic due to AI chatbots and summaries, right now, to the point that Google itself saw its ad revenue growth drop. İçöz acknowledged that people are making websites with ChatGPT or Claude now as compared to deploying something on WordPress, and he said some sites won’t need a content management system at all as the web expands.
Spacefast comes amid turbulent months at Automattic. In an OpenAI/Sam Altman-style saga, the company’s board forced CEO Matt Mullenweg out, but he was back in control within days. The rebel board was eventually replaced, and the interim CFO left within weeks of appointment. In October, TechCrunch reported that the company had begun layoffs across several properties and more cuts were expected.

articles.title: China exports, imports soar past expectations in October — surplus narrows sharply
articles.text:
China's exports and imports surged more than expected in October, while its surplus shrank sharply, undershooting expectations even as it crossed $1 trillion for the year so far.
Goods exports soared by 35.2% last month from a year earlier, according to the official data released Tuesday, exceeding expectations for a 33.5% jump in a Reuters poll, but slowing from the 36.3% growth in September.
Imports climbed by 41.6% last month, customs data showed, jumping from 31% in September and sharply beating estimates for a 32% rise by analysts polled by Reuters.
The monthly surplus dropped to $105.3 billion in October, the lowest level since April, according to LSEG data, with the year-to-date figure at $1.04 trillion, compared with a record $1.2 trillion for the full year 2025. Calls from trading partners have grown louder for Beijing to boost domestic demand and balance its economy.
The strength in exports has allowed policymakers to continue relying on moderate policy support to meet the country's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%. Household consumption has remained soft, with retail sales growing a modest 1.1% in September, underscoring the imbalance in the world's second-largest economy.
Much of the surge in exports reflects robust demand for its chips and other artificial intelligence-related hardware. But any slowdown in the global AI buildout would risk denting the momentum and squeezing Chinese exporters' margins.
A separate survey by China Beige Book showed new domestic and export orders for goods slowed in October compared to a year earlier. Factory activity also unexpectedly shrank last month, according to official PMI data, as overseas orders cooled. "The stronger side of the economy got weaker," the New York-headquartered research firm said in a note on Oct. 30.
Washington and Beijing agreed in September to extend a broader trade truce by two months to January, along with a slew of other trade measures, including export-control waivers for certain critical minerals and special port fees for each other's vessels.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are expected to meet for a third time this year at the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China next week.
The European Union also reached an agreement with Beijing last month to limit the imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles over the next few years, as part of the effort to reduce its trade deficit with Beijing.
But the auto import curbs, taking effect on Dec.1, would barely contain China's export boom, according to analysts.
The cap of 350,000 imported cars per year is above the 300,000 hybrids that China exported to Europe last year, though well below the 800,000 units in annualized pace over the last three months, according to Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
"Europe still is a long way from a coherent trade and industrial policy with respect to autos, let alone a coherent economic policy towards overall trade with China," said Setser, a former U.S. Treasury official who specializes in global trade and capital flows.
Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that the official data was released on Tuesday.

articles.title: SoftBank Group shares surge 11% as Asian tech stocks track Wall Street rebound
articles.text:
Asian technology stocks surged Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight as a sharp decline in oil prices lifted sentiment while renewed buying in chip names spilled over into Asia, following last week's bruising sell-off.
Japan's technology investment giant SoftBank Group surged 12%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest gained 5.41%. Semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron rose 5.88%, while Lasertec and Disco advanced 6.34% and 6.95%, respectively.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 8.01%, while Samsung Electronics rose 5.32%. Samsung SDI climbed 6.27%.
The gains followed a strong session on Wall Street, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.35% to clock its best day since April 8.
The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week, fueled by concerns that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially impacting demand for artificial intelligence chips and infrastructure.
Beyond the political uncertainty surrounding potential restrictions on data-center development, investors have also grown increasingly wary of the enormous capital expenditures required to build out AI infrastructure. Questions over how quickly those investments will translate into meaningful profits have weighed on sentiment toward companies across the semiconductor supply chain.

articles.title: Senate advances Trump-backed bipartisan bill to speed critical infrastructure projects
articles.text:
The Senate on Monday advanced a bipartisan bill that aims to significantly speed up the approval process for critical U.S. infrastructure projects.
The vote, 73-25, allows the Senate to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act bill as it heads toward final passage
The bill, which would reform the permitting process for projects, has emerged as a key priority of Congress' lame duck session. President Donald Trump, who often opposes bipartisan legislation, has endorsed the package.
The legislation would amend laws like the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act to speed up the review process that hinders the buildout of resources like electricity generation, while also overhauling the process for greenlighting transmission lines.
The bill would also force artificial intelligence companies and data center developers to pay their own way for power and grid enhancements.
Republicans have long argued that environmental laws are too restrictive and hinder the U.S. from building big things like power plants and mines. Democrats, meanwhile, want to speed up the buildout of clean energy projects like solar and wind to lower carbon emissions
Lawmakers have circled a deal to streamline the nation's complex web of permitting laws for years, but most prior efforts have sputtered. This year, negotiators believe they will catch lightning in a bottle and make BAAJA law before this Congress ends in January.
The lawmakers are touting further tailwinds after last week's elections, where Democrats wiped out Republicans and seized majorities in both chambers of Congress
"Just one week ago Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do," said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the top Democrat and likely incoming Chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, during a Monday morning press conference.
The bill would still require approval by the House of Representatives if it is able to pass the Senate this week. Trump's endorsement of the effort is likely to help the bill get a vote in the House if it clears the Senate.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says Anthropic's IPO could make or break the AI trade. Here's why
articles.text:
Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Monday.
"Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," the "Mad Money" host said, exactly two weeks after the Claude developer filed its S-1 IPO paperwork. Despite the recent sell-off in AI stocks, Anthropic is reportedly moving ahead with its IPO plans. The company is expected to meet with major investors this week and is targeting a trading debut as early as Thursday or Friday of next week, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "I don't think it's hyperbolic to say that this could be one of the most consequential IPOs in history."
Cramer explained that the billions of dollars being spent on AI chips and data centers ultimately depend on a handful of AI developers, including Anthropic, generating enough revenue to justify those investments.
"Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending," Cramer said. "If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today."
Cramer pointed to SpaceX as an example of how interconnected the AI trade has become. Much of the Elon Musk rocket and AI company's recent revenue growth has come from renting computing capacity to customers, including Alphabet's Google and Anthropic. Google pays roughly $900 million a month for that capacity, while Anthropic's commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion monthly to more than $3 billion, according to its IPO prospectus.
Those contracts allow for SpaceX's massive purchases of Nvidia chips. "But if an Anthropic deal fails?" Cramer said. "Then Anthropic wouldn't have the cash to fulfill its contracts, and you'd have to take down estimates for both SpaceX and Nvidia, along with a whole host of other compute providers to Anthropic, and their suppliers." Not to mention, Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia have all invested in Anthropic, making their earnings sensitive to changes in the AI developer's valuation.
The wrinkle here is that investor appetite for an Anthropic IPO appears to be weakening. Anthropic's potential valuation has reportedly fallen from as much as $2 trillion earlier this fall to as low as $1 trillion following last week's technology sell-off on concerns that the Democratic wave in the midterm election will mean slower new data center construction.
On Friday, during the CNBC Investing Club's Annual Meeting, Cramer also stressed the importance of the Anthropic offering to the AI trade and to Club portfolio names Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says Nvidia investors need to prepare for a future without Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Mad Money
Jim Cramer says Nvidia investors need to prepare for a future without Jensen Huang
Key Points
- Jim Cramer warned that this long-standing "own it, don't trade it" status for Nvidia's stock could be at risk amid uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang's future.
- Cramer remains confident in Nvidia's technology, but warned that growing opposition to data centers and financing challenges could threaten demand for its AI chips.
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday that uncertainty surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the data center boom has raised new risks for the artificial intelligence chipmaker's stock. Cramer's comments follow Sunday's news that Nvidia's board is investigating Huang over his extramarital affair with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, who is suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of spying for China. Though Huang remains CEO, the investigation has raised questions about his future at the company . "Given the facts of the story, which seem to get worse with each update, we are going to have to consider owning shares in a Jensen-less Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "If that is the case, you can no longer be bound by our 'own it, don't trade it' mantra, which has been the default view of the CNBC Investing Club." Nvidia shares tumbled more than 4% Monday, even as the broader market rallied, extending a sell-off that has erased roughly 22% of the chipmaker's value over the past month. Prior to Monday, Nvidia's decline has coincided with weakness in the broader AI build-out trade. "What you need to know is that Nvidia is a less attractive stock than it was a week ago, even as I think the business remains strong," Cramer said. "That was true before this weekend's revelations about spies and affairs, based solely on the election results, but if Jensen's transgressions mean he can no longer lead this company, that only makes matters worse." But that doesn't necessarily mean it's time to sell Nvidia, according to Cramer, whose Charitable Trust, the portfolio used by the Investing Club, first bought shares of the chipmaker in 2017. It has maintained a consistent position since early 2019. Cramer pointed to Apple's success under Tim Cook following Steve Jobs ' death as evidence that companies can thrive after losing visionary leaders. Cramer's Charitable Trust has owned Apple for more than a decade. "We are not anxious to dump [Nvidia]," Cramer said about his Charitable Trust, citing what he believes to be Nvidia's deep management bench and established technological leadership . "I think Nvidia can go forward just on the strength of its multiyear product map," he added. The increased uncertainty, nevertheless, comes at a challenging time for Nvidia, as political opposition to data centers threatens to slow the massive infrastructure build-out that has fueled demand for its chips and turned the company into one of the world's most valuable enterprises. Cramer said a potential moderation in data center construction poses greater risks for smaller, heavily indebted neoclouds such as CoreWeave , Nebius and Iren , which rely on outside capital to expand their computing capacity. As of June 30, Nvidia had equity stakes in CoreWeave and Nebius, according to its 13F securities securities filing . In May, Nvidia announced a partnership with Iren that included warrants for up to 30 million shares. "I think these marginal buyers of Nvidia chips may not be able to get the financing they need to build data centers on their own," Cramer said. Without those companies expanding aggressively, demand for Nvidia's chips could become increasingly dependent on the spending plans of established hyperscalers such as Amazon and Microsoft .
